### 0.0 ⚠ A `§6` DEVIATION, RULED 2026-10-31 — Task 8b runs in parallel with 8a's last review round

`§6`'s order rule is *no task starts before the previous one is green and tagged*. **Task 8b
(`QRPAGER-23`) is starting while `task-8a` is NOT tagged, and that is Muhammad's ruling of 2026-10-31,
recorded here before the first implementation commit rather than discovered in the history.**

**What is outstanding on 8a, and what is not.** `§5`'s *"AND CI RUNS IT AS A SECOND JOB"* is
**discharged** — run **#151**, commit `d8c9652`, branch `task-8a-design-system`, conclusion **SUCCESS**,
7m 05s, reported by Muhammad from the Actions list (this machine has no Actions access: `gh` absent, both
token variables unset, private repo → HTTP 404; the same provenance as `§4a`'s Task 0 row, *"run #2, both
jobs green, 37s"*). **What remains is one review round on the fix diff** — `a1f1263..d8c9652`, 18 commits
of fix work that no reviewer has read, which `§11`'s round limit allows and requires.

**The reason, stated as what it is: speed, chosen knowingly.** 8b's work does not depend on the outcome of
that review — it builds on the token toolchain, not on the twenty fixes the review will read — so
serialising the two would cost a task's latency for a dependency that does not exist.

**THE CONDITION THAT MAKES IT SAFE, and it is a hard one:** 8b never edits a line that
`a1f1263..d8c9652` changed. It builds **additively** — new gate steps, new `ARTEFACTS` entries, new
assertions, new files — on the token toolchain, the artefact registry and the gate scripts. A scope item
that cannot be done without editing one of those lines is a **stop-and-report**, not an edit. Measured,
that diff touches **67 files**, and for the files it CREATED every line is a changed line, so those get a
sibling rather than a modification:

```
git diff --name-only a1f1263..d8c9652        # the 67, re-derivable in one command
```

**THE ONE COST, named in advance:** if the fix-diff review forces a code change in 8a, **this branch
rebases.** That is the whole exposure, it is bounded by the additive condition above, and it is accepted.

**The branch.** Work proceeds on **`task-8b-precoding`**, whose base `git merge-base` confirms **is**
`d8c9652` — exactly where the tag will land — so these commits and a later cut from the tag produce
**identical history**. No branch is cut from a loose sha and nothing waits for the tag. When the tag
lands at `d8c9652`: `task-8b-panel-restyle` is cut from it, these commits **fast-forward with no
rebase**, and the holding name retires. The branch history's one explanation is
`docs/tickets/QRPAGER-23.md §10`.

Filament's own resolver clears AA on all twelve resolved pairs (six families, both modes) at
**5.15 to 7.54** against the one-liner's **3.43 FAIL**. `warning` anchors at shade 400 rather
than 600 — measured, 600 reproduced `danger`'s 3.68 failure, and `alert-fill`'s own approval
bounds it to text at ≥ 24px. `info` is the neutral ramp, identical to `gray`, because the
approved palette has no informational colour and our panels request one nowhere.

**`R-118`'s four computed-style clauses are CLOSED**, measured in Chromium over the compiled
panel theme and Filament's own markup — 10 browser checks across two motion projects. Clause 2
cost a real fix: Filament's controls render at **32–40px** against `§12`'s 44px bar, so
`resources/css/filament/targets.css` applies `min-height: var(--target-min)` as a floor to eleven
standalone control classes, derived from six real renders and held to them by `PanelTargetTest`.
The four it deliberately does not cover are `R-174`.

**The finding, in one line:** Filament's only sanctioned colour extension point either DISCARDS the
approved value or demands eleven values per family that nobody has approved — and its one-line form
produces a dark-mode button at **3.43:1**, which fails WCAG AA for text.

`Color::generatePalette()` keeps only the HUE of the hex it is given; lightness and chroma are
Filament's own constants at every shade. So `brand #0B6B4F` appears at no shade, `ink` (hue 165.122)
and `brand` (hue 166.529) produce indistinguishable ladders, and a chroma below 0.03 collapses to
grey. The shades are not decorative: `ButtonComponentColorMap` runs `calculateContrastRatio` over the
whole palette at the 4.5 bar and picks bg/hover/text from it, and a MISSING shade silently becomes
white rather than erroring.

**The recommendation is inside an already-approved mechanism.** Derive an 11-shade ladder per family
from the approved value by 8a's ruled `mix(from, to, amount%) in
srgb-8bit-component-linear-round-half-up`, anchored so that **shade 600 is the approved value itself**
— which is the shade Filament's light-mode button asks for. Driven through Filament's own resolver,
that puts `#0B6B4F` on the button in both modes at **6.50:1**, against the one-liner's shade-400 pick
and its failing dark pair.

**And one thing it does not settle, stated rather than glossed:** `alert-fill`'s derived ladder gives
a dark pair of **3.68**, below the bar. The token source already says a fill *"is read against its own
text, not against the ground"* and names `alert-ink` as its partner, so `danger` needs either a tuned
mix or an explicit text partner — a second decision inside the first.

**The full measurement, the ruling and what the measurement decided that the ruling left open
are in `docs/tickets/QRPAGER-23.md §0 SR-4`** — including the two caps, the per-family anchors,
and why `border-strong` is not an eligible anchor.

### 0.0f ⚠⚠⚠ THE TAGGING PROCEDURE — MUHAMMAD, 2026-11-07, RANK-1, STANDING FROM NOW ON

**His instruction, verbatim:** *"MAKE THIS THE LAST MOVE. From now on the order is: get a
green CI run at the candidate commit FIRST, then tag that sha. Tagging and then discovering
the tag-ref run fails is what cost two force-pushes here. Write that into `PLAN §0` as the
tagging procedure."*

**THE ORDER, AND IT IS NOT NEGOTIABLE:**

1. Finish the work. The **last non-docs commit** is the one the gates are measured at.
2. Run the gates and write `§0`'s *Next up* clause: `Gates measured at <that sha>`, the
   totals, and the transcripts — **as a docs commit**.
3. **Push the branch and get a GREEN four-job CI run at the candidate commit.** The candidate
   is that docs commit, not the code commit.
4. **Only then** tag that exact sha: annotated, `--cleanup=verbatim`, the message
   byte-identical to `docs/tickets/QRPAGER-<key>-tag-message.txt`.
5. Push the tag and read the **tag-ref** run green with `gh`. Record its run id in `§0`.

**⚠ WHY STEP 3 COMES BEFORE STEP 4, measured rather than asserted.** `task-12` was tagged
first and moved twice, which cost two force-pushes he had to approve one at a time:

| tag at | `records:check` at that tree | tag-ref run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `73b4b55` | passed | **`42384449982` FAILED** — `ci-parity.test.mjs:329`, `R-245` |
| `204cd43` | **fails** `records(b3)` | **`42390425126` FAILED** |
| `1256c37` | exit 0, and `42392610953` green on the branch first | **green** |

**⚠⚠ AND THE SHARPEST PART: A TAG CAN NEVER SIT ON A CODE COMMIT IN THIS REPOSITORY.**
`records(b3)` requires `§0`'s `Gates measured at <sha>` to have **nothing outside `docs/`
changed since**. A code commit's own `§0` cannot name itself — `checkStatedHead`'s docblock
says why: *"a file cannot state the sha of the commit that contains it — writing the sha
changes it."* So the only commit whose tree can satisfy its own provenance check is a
**docs-only commit after the last code commit**. `204cd43` was a code commit, and that is
the whole reason its tag-ref run could not be made green by any ordering. `task-10`'s tag is
on such a docs commit, which is why its tag-ref run went green and `task-11`'s did not.

**⚠ A GREEN BRANCH RUN DOES NOT CLOSE A TASK.** His words from the same ruling: *"The whole
point is a delivery record whose own CI passes, so a green branch run does not close this."*
The branch run and the tag-ref run execute the same tree through **different refs**, and
`check-records` reads the repository's tags — so they are genuinely different measurements,
which is exactly what `R-245` is about.

**⚠ AND TWO EARLIER TAGS ARE LEFT RED ON PURPOSE.** `task-11` (`41627842991`) and `task-11a`
(`41651378270`, then `41655058406`) have failing tag-ref runs and are **not** re-tagged. His
ruling: *"re-tagging them at a commit carrying a fix made after them would make them certify
something that was not true when they were cut … A delivery record is allowed to contain a
known, explained failure — it is not allowed to contain a rewritten one."* `R-245` carries the
cause and the fixing commit.

#### (a2) ⚠ WHERE THIS FILE ACTUALLY LIVES, and why `R-001`'s doc exception does not describe it

Added 2026-10-31 by Task 8b's pre-coding gate, because it was discovered by trying to follow the rule.

**`R-001`'s settled exception says a documentation-only commit — `docs/**`, including this file — goes
straight to `main`, no branch, no PR. That does not describe the STATE FILE.** The authoritative copy of
`docs/PLAN.md` lives on an **unmerged task branch**, not on `main`:

```
$ git log --oneline origin/main..task-8a-design-system -- docs/PLAN.md | wc -l
81
```

**Eighty-one commits to this file that `main` has never seen.** `main` is reserved until client handover
(`§10`), the task branches are not merged by instruction, and every task since Task 3 has updated `§0` and
`§4a` on its own branch. So **whoever reads `PLAN.md` on `main` reads a record four tasks old** — Task 3's
— while believing they are reading the file whose own header calls itself *"the only place that states
current state"*.

**The consequence that bites, and it is why this is a note rather than a shrug:** a `PLAN` edit made on
`main` in good faith, following `R-001` to the letter, would **fork the state file** — two divergent
copies of the one document this project uses to answer *where are we*. Task 8b's `§3` answers hit exactly
this and held the edit on a task branch instead (`QRPAGER-23 §10`).

**The honest reading of `R-001`'s exception, until it is amended:** it is sound for a doc that is *about*
a moment (an evidence transcript, a ticket's answers) and unsound for a doc that *is* the project's
state. The exception's own stated reason — *"`§0` in particular has to be editable the moment state
changes"* — is the argument for editing `§0` on whichever branch holds the live copy, which is the
opposite of what its letter says. **Amending it is a rank-2-adjacent call and is Muhammad's**; what is
recorded here is the measurement and the trap, so the next person to follow the rule reads this first.

#### (b) Cannot be checked from here — what to look at, and the right answer

**W-0 · ⚠ REVOKE THE GITHUB PAT PASTED INTO THE SESSION ON 2026-10-26. Delete this item once done.**
*What:* a fine-grained token beginning `github_pat_11AZ3S5…` was pasted into a Claude Code session as
plaintext, to authenticate `gh`. Revoke it at **github.com → Settings → Developer settings → Personal
access tokens → Fine-grained tokens**, and issue a replacement only by a route that does not cross a
transcript. *Why no agent:* only the token's owner can revoke it. *Why it must be revoked rather than
kept:* the session transcript is written to disk
(`~/.claude/projects/…/<session>.jsonl`, confirmed to contain it), and `/export` writes the whole
transcript into the working tree — it did exactly that once this session, as `apps/api/report.md`. That
file was deleted and `report.md` is now git-ignored, and the token never reached a commit (`gitleaks
detect` over all 83 commits: no leaks), but a secret that has been written to a file on disk is spent.
*How verified:* the token is absent from the fine-grained token list, and any `gh` call using it answers
`HTTP 401`. *The safe replacement route:* install `gh`, then run `gh auth login` **interactively** —
typing `! gh auth login` at the prompt — so the token is entered into `gh`'s own prompt and never appears
as command text. Never `--with-token` from a pasted string.

**W-1 · Paste the repo copy over the claude.ai Project instructions.**
*What:* replace the Project-instructions copy of `PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md` **wholesale** with the current
repo file. *Why no agent:* the Project instructions live in the claude.ai Project, not the filesystem — no
session can read or write them, which is also why the drift was invisible. *How verified:* search the
pasted copy for four phrases — `Relay rule`, `Round limit`, `repo guard in CI`, `or in an error response
body`. Four searches, four hits.

**Wholesale, not paragraph by paragraph, and the count is the argument.** The repo copy has gained

### The eighth review — the bar, set before it ran

> Written here verbatim, by the user, **before** the review was commissioned, so that what counts as
> blocking was not decided under fatigue after reading its findings.

> "Eighth review, final. Blocking: only a cross-tenant read or write reachable WITHOUT a raw set_config in a
> callback — that is, a failure of the invariant Task 1 exists to guarantee. Everything else, at any severity,
> goes to §5 with an owner and a date. Seven reviews have confirmed tenant isolation holds; the findings since
> the fifth round are durability, message content and record accuracy, each round of fixing which has produced
> more. The branch ships on the invariant, with the remainder documented."

Each ticket carries its own acceptance gate **copied verbatim from §3 below**, the §6 pre-coding questions as a checklist, an explicit _out of scope_ table naming which task owns each excluded item, and the known traps for that task. Tickets are linked `blocks` in order.

### How a task runs

1. Open the ticket. Read `PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md`, this file, `docs/adr/`.
   **Including `§3.1` and `§3.2` for this task's own row** — what the gate still needs, and which
   `§5` rows the task owns with whether its gate could catch them. Task 2 began with `§0` naming 6
   debt items while `§5`'s owner column assigned 17, and nobody noticed until both were read.
2. Answer the seven §6 pre-coding questions **as a comment on the ticket**. Then move to In Progress.
3. Branch `task-N-<slug>`. Build. Three gates green against real Postgres + Redis.
   **Push at ROUND BOUNDARIES, not per commit** — see `§0.2` (c); every push now gets its own CI verdict.
4. PR. Both required checks green.
5. **QA Review** — separate agent session, diff + ticket only.
6. **Security Review** — separate agent session, diff + ticket only.
   **Run 5 and 6 AT THE SAME TIME, each in its own slot** — `tools/gate/bin/reviewer-slot`, see `§0.2` (b).
7. Every Critical and High fixed with a regression test. Medium / Low → §5 with owner and date.
8. **FINAL EVIDENCE, ONCE, after the LAST fix round** — `tools/gate/bin/final-evidence`, see `§0.2` (a).
   Then squash merge, tag `task-N`, push the tag.
9. **Update §0 of this file, and §4a with the gate evidence.**

### 0.2 Standing practice — three repo changes made 2026-11-01, so Tasks 10-14 cost less than Task 9

Ruled by Muhammad on 2026-11-01, after Task 9 took four hours and two `§11` rounds. **Each is a repo
change rather than advice**, and each is recorded here rather than in `QRPAGER-16`, because a practice
written into one ticket is a practice the next task does not inherit. The step list above is amended to
match; this subsection is the reasoning.

**(a) FINAL EVIDENCE ONCE — `tools/gate/bin/final-evidence`.**
Task 9 produced its three-green-runs, both fresh-clone proofs and the Lighthouse measurement **once per
review round** — three times, and only the last set was ever cited. `PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md §6` asks for
the evidence; it nowhere asks for it per round. And the early sets were not merely wasted: evidence taken
*before* a fix round describes a tree the round then changed, which is `§11` round one's **QA H-4**
exactly — a figure measured against a parent that has since moved. So the five artefacts are now one
command, run once, after the last fix round, in a fixed order, with the two heavy gates strictly
sequential (`R-200`'s mechanism one layer out: the suite and the E2E share Redis). **It REFUSES a dirty
tree** rather than warning about one, because the whole artefact is a claim about a single commit;
`--allow-dirty` exists for a rehearsal and stamps the transcript as one.

⚠ **AND (b3) HAS AN ORDERING CONSTRAINT THAT COST A GATE RUN ON THE NIGHT IT WAS WRITTEN — STATE THE
SHA BEFORE YOU MEASURE, NEVER AFTER.** `records:check` is a step of `pnpm gate`, and (b3) compares `§0`'s
provenance sha against `HEAD`. So the moment any non-`docs/` file changes, the gate CANNOT go green until
`§0` names the new sha — and `§0` cannot honestly name a *measured* sha until the gate is green. That is a
deadlock if the two are done in the wrong order, and it is not a defect in either half. The order that
works, and the only one:

1. make every code change and commit it → sha `X`;
2. restate `§0`'s provenance to `X` and commit that **alone**, docs-only → sha `Y`;
3. run the gate at `Y`. (b3) sees stated `X`, `HEAD` `Y`, and a diff confined to `docs/` — which is exactly
   the property it checks, so it passes, and the figures legitimately describe `X`'s code.

⚠ **AND (b4) HAS A BOOTSTRAPPING WRINKLE OF THE SAME FAMILY — THE TRANSCRIPT AND THE FIGURE MUST MOVE
TOGETHER.** (b4) compares `§0`'s stated test count against the committed transcript, and `records:check`
is step 4 of `pnpm gate` — **before** Vitest. So when the count CHANGES, the new transcript can only come
from a green run, the run dies at step 4 because `§0` and the old transcript disagree, and `§0` cannot
honestly state a figure no transcript yet supports. The way through is again the order, not an exemption:
state the OLD figure in the working tree only, run the gate to green, then commit the new transcript and
the new figure **in one commit**. The inconsistent intermediate state is never committed, so the record
never carries a number it cannot support. Measured on 2026-11-02 when two new test cases took the suites
1173 → 1175 and 814 → 817.

**Both wrinkles share one root, and it is worth naming:** (b3) and (b4) are steps of the very gate whose
output they describe, so they are self-referential by construction. That is not a reason to weaken either
— each caught a real defect the night it was written — but the ordering it forces has to be written down
rather than rediscovered at 3am by the next session.

⚠ **WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE ABOUT IT:** exempting "figure-irrelevant" paths like `.gitignore` from
(b3). A one-line `.gitignore` fix did oblige a full re-measure, and the friction is real — but a list of
paths that do not count is precisely the narrow-the-assertion move `PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md §8` forbids,
and the first entry on such a list is never the last. If the friction outweighs the staleness it prevents,
the honest fix is a tighter SCOPE — `§0` naming the sha its **gate figures** were measured at, and (b3)
checking only the paths those gates actually read — not an exceptions list. Muhammad's call; recorded
rather than taken.

**(b) REVIEWERS IN PARALLEL — `tools/gate/bin/reviewer-slot`, proven by `apps/api/bin/parallel-reviewer-proof`.**
Task 9's two reviewers ran **sequentially**, and so did 8a's and 8b's, for the reason the builder report
gave: *"both worktrees share this machine's one Postgres and one Redis"* (`R-200`). That was never a
property of the reviews — it was two runners pointed at `qrpager_test` and Redis db 0. A slot gives each
worktree its own `DB_DATABASE` (`qrpager_test_s<N>`, which `db:bootstrap` creates) and its own
`REDIS_DB`/`REDIS_CACHE_DB` pair, all three of which the application already read from the environment.
**Two things had to be verified rather than assumed.** `phpunit.xml`'s
`<env name="DB_DATABASE" value="qrpager_test"/>` carries no `force` attribute, and PHPUnit's own
`TextUI/Configuration/PhpHandler.php:167` reads `if ($force || getenv($name) === false)` — so an exported
value wins and the file's is the fallback. And **`TestCase`'s suite lock had to move**: it took
`pg_advisory_lock(2_000_000_049)`, one constant for every runner, so two slots would have queued on it
however separate their data was. It is now keyed by the test database's own name
(`TestCase::suiteLockKey()`), still above `2_000_000_000` by construction because `RoleTimeoutTest` draws
from `random_int(1, 2_000_000_000)` and this lock is never released. **The proof asserts OVERLAP, not two
green exits** — `concurrent-suite-proof`'s own header says the second runner used to *queue*, and two
queued green runs look identical to two isolated ones if the only assertion is the exit code.

**(c) STOP PUSHING PER COMMIT — `ci.yml`'s `cancel-in-progress` narrowed to pull requests.**
`concurrency.cancel-in-progress` was `github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' && !startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/')`,
which is **true for every task branch**. Task 9 pushed once per commit, so each push cancelled the run
about to deliver the previous commit's verdict: a wall of `Cancelled` that reads as failure, with no
individual commit holding a verdict at all. ⚠ **MEASURED rather than described, 2026-11-01:** of the
**15 most recent runs on this branch, 12 are `cancelled`** and the other 3 are `failure` — `#177` to
`#186` is an unbroken run of ten — so for most of the task the branch page carried no verdict worth
reading, which is why `#187`'s red went unexamined until a cold session was told to look. That is the `task-1` cancellation reproduced on a task branch.
**Of the two options, the repo change was taken rather than the discipline** — *push only at round
boundaries* is a rule somebody has to remember, and `R-126`, `W-14` and the `task-1` merge are three
instances of the same forgetting; `PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md §7` says a recurrence means the mechanism was
missing. So only a `pull_request` ref cancels now, main and tags keep their verdicts as before, and a task
branch gets one verdict per push. ⚠ **AND THE CLAIM *"a verdict per push"* IS WRONG, CORRECTED 2026-11-02 BY MEASURING IT.** GitHub allows only ONE run to be **pending** in a concurrency group, and a newer pending run supersedes the older one whatever `cancel-in-progress` says. Measured on this branch: **`#190` was `in_progress` and SURVIVED `#191`'s push** — which the old expression would have killed — while **`#191` was still `pending` and was `cancelled` when `#192` entered the group.** So what the change buys, stated honestly: **a run that has STARTED is never killed, and the NEWEST HEAD always gets a verdict.** An intermediate commit pushed in quick succession can still lose its own. That makes *push at round boundaries* a real part of the mechanism rather than a courtesy: batching is what keeps each pushed commit the newest head long enough to be verified. **The step list above still says push at round boundaries**, because the
CI-minute cost is real and batching is the cheaper habit — the difference is that forgetting it now costs
minutes instead of costing the verdict.

## 2. Data contract — filled at Task 1

> Blueprint §3.1 is superseded (C3). **The Laravel migrations in `apps/api/database/migrations` are the
> source of truth; this section transcribes them.** Any task that needs a new table, column, enum value,
> role, GUC or grant updates this section **first** (`PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md §6.1`) and then writes the
> migration. Nothing here may be invented by a later task.

### 2.1 Roles and connections

Four roles exist in the cluster, but only **three are application roles** — the fourth is the cluster's
pre-existing bootstrap superuser, which exists whether or not we name it.

| Role             | Attributes                                                                                         | Used by                                                        | Laravel connection        |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `qrpager_root`   | SUPERUSER (local) / `rds_superuser` (Aurora)                                                       | **Role and database bootstrap only**, never by the application | `pgsql_root`              |
| `qrpager_owner`  | NOSUPERUSER **NOBYPASSRLS** NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE, owns every table, `CREATE` on `schema public` | Migrations only                                                | `pgsql_owner`             |
| `qrpager_app`    | NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE, **no `CREATE` on any schema**                     | Web requests                                                   | `pgsql` ← **the default** |
| `qrpager_worker` | same attributes as `qrpager_app`                                                                   | Queue worker                                                   | `pgsql_worker`            |

**Why `root` is separate from `owner`.** Verified in-session: a Postgres **superuser ignores `ENABLE` and
`FORCE` row level security entirely** — it read both tenants' rows with no tenant context set. Task 0's
container bootstrapped its superuser _as_ `qrpager_owner`, so the §3 gate clause "`owner` is also bound by
FORCE RLS" was unsatisfiable by construction. The bootstrap superuser is therefore renamed `qrpager_root`
and `qrpager_owner` is created as a **non-superuser** table owner. This maps to production exactly: the
Aurora master user bootstraps the roles once, migrations run as `owner`, and neither is the runtime role.

`DB_OWNER_*` and `DB_ROOT_*` credentials belong **only** to the migration/CI environment, and a runtime task
should carry `DB_USERNAME=qrpager_app` (or `qrpager_worker`) and nothing else.

**Corrected 2026-10-25 (F6, security review of task-1).** This paragraph used to claim that
`assertSafeRuntimeRole()` "fails the boot if it ever carries more". It does not, and never did. What exists
is narrower: the guard asks **one connection** for its `current_user` and refuses a role that can see past
row level security — owner, superuser, `BYPASSRLS`, or a member of the owner. It does **not** inspect the
environment, so a runtime task that also carries `DB_OWNER_PASSWORD` passes it; and `withoutTenantScope()`
is a global function defaulting to the owner connection, so request-handling code is one call from a
cross-tenant bypass that is audited but not prevented. Nothing calls the guard yet either. Both halves —
wiring it into boot, and widening it to refuse a resolvable non-runtime credential — are **Task 2's**, whose
gate carries "boot refuses a runtime task that can resolve owner or root credentials".

### 2.2 GUCs — the only two that exist (C1)

| GUC                 | Scope                                                                             | Set by                                                                        | Read by                            |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `app.tenant_id`     | **transaction-local always** — `SELECT set_config('app.tenant_id', ?, true)` (C2) | `withTenant()`                                                                | every tenant policy                |
| `app.bypass_tenant` | transaction-local | **two setters, and only these two:** `withoutTenantScope()` — owner connection only, writes an `audit_log` row — **and** the body of each `§2.8` `SECURITY DEFINER` resolver, which turns it on for the duration of its own body and restores the previous value before returning. The second arrived with Task 3 (`resolve_pager_token`); this cell named only the first until 2026-10-27, although `§2.8` has prescribed the other since Task 1 | the `owner_bypass_*` policies only |

**Verified, and the reason the `NULLIF` guard is not optional:** a placeholder GUC that has _never_ been set
returns `NULL`, but once a transaction has set it, **every later transaction on that connection reads an
empty string `''`** — and `''::uuid` raises `22P02`, it does not match nothing. Every policy therefore uses
`NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid`, which yields `NULL`, which makes the policy
false, which is "**0 rows, no error**".

**`app.bypass_tenant` is not a general escape hatch.** Every `owner_bypass_*` policy is `TO qrpager_owner`.
Verified: `qrpager_app` setting `app.bypass_tenant = 'on'` itself still reads **0 rows**. SQL injection in
the web tier therefore cannot reach another tenant's data — the GUC is inert for the runtime roles.

### 2.3 Enum types — one source, mechanically checked

The **PHP enum is the source**. The Postgres type is a native `ENUM` created by migration, and
`tests/Feature/Database/EnumContractTest.php` compares `pg_enum` labels against the PHP cases for every
pair in `App\Domain\DatabaseEnums::map()`, so adding a case to either side fails the build until both
agree. Task 8 generates `packages/contracts` from the same registry (ADR-003) — never a hand-written copy.

| Postgres type      | PHP enum                          | Values (ordered)                                            |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pager_status`     | `App\Domain\Pager\PagerStatus`    | `waiting` · `ready` · `completed` · `cancelled` · `expired` |
| `outbox_status`    | `App\Domain\Outbox\OutboxStatus`  | `pending` · `sent` · `dead`                                 |
| `tenant_status`    | `App\Domain\Tenancy\TenantStatus` | `active` · `suspended`                                      |
| `tenant_role`      | `App\Domain\Tenancy\TenantRole`   | `owner` · `manager` · `staff`                               |
| `audit_actor_type` | `App\Domain\Audit\AuditActorType` | `user` · `system` · `platform`                              |

`tenant_role` holds **tenant-scoped** roles only. Transitions of `pager_status` are defined in the PHP enum
by Task 3, not here.

**The platform-admin flag landed at Task 5 and it is NOT a fourth `tenant_role` value** — this paragraph
used to say "is Task 5's and is not in this contract yet", and the resolution is that it never belongs in
this table. It is `users.is_platform_admin boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false` (`§2.4`). A `platform_admin`
member of `tenant_role` could only ever be stored in `tenant_users.role`, which requires a `tenant_id`, so
the value would exist only attached to a tenant — which is exactly what a platform admin is not (`§2.4`:
"platform staff belong to none"). **Task 5 also adds two enum-shaped contracts that are deliberately NOT
Postgres types:** `App\Domain\Auth\Principal` (`platform_admin · owner · manager · staff · device`), the
authorisation subject, which exists only in PHP because two of its five cases are not roles at all — one is
the boolean above and one is a credential shape (a KDS device token) — and `App\Domain\Auth\Ability`, a
capability vocabulary rather than a stored value. Keeping the five principals in one PHP enum is what lets
the role matrix be one array over all of them without putting either case in the data contract.

**One type joined at Task 6:** `provisioning_status` — `pending`, `running`, `completed`, `failed` —
mirrored by `App\Domain\Provisioning\ProvisioningStatus`, registered in `DatabaseEnums::map()` so
`EnumContractTest` fails on drift in either direction. Its transition table lives on the PHP enum, as
`PagerStatus`' does, so the panel, the provisioning job and the tests read one source. `running -> pending`
is the one judgement call: a job killed mid-flight leaves the row at `running`, and the only way a later run
may pick it up is to put it back — `attempts` is what stops that being a loop. `completed` is terminal with
no exit at all, because a provisioned tenant's id is already taken and the insert that would re-provision it
raises `23505`.

**Two types joined at Task 7**, both registered in `DatabaseEnums::map()` for the same reason:

| Postgres type         | PHP enum                                   | Values (ordered)                                                                            |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `landing_page_status` | `App\Domain\Landing\LandingPageStatus`    | `draft` · `published`                                                                        |
| `domain_status`       | `App\Domain\Landing\DomainStatus`         | `pending_dns` · `dns_verified` · `certificate_pending` · `active` · `redirecting` · `failed` |

`landing_page_status` has **two** values and not three, and the absent one is named here because its
absence is the design: there is no `publishing` state. A publish is `§6.6`'s write-new-then-switch — the
immutable snapshot is written first, the stable pointer last, and the database row last of all — so there
is no moment at which the row is a third thing. A status that existed only inside a transaction would be a
status no reader could ever observe, and a crash would strand rows in it.

`domain_status`' transitions live on the PHP enum, as `PagerStatus`' and `ProvisioningStatus`' do. Three of
them are worth stating here because they are the falsifiable half of `§3` row 7 under the task's SR-2:
`pending_dns -> dns_verified` requires a recorded `dns_verified_at`, `certificate_pending -> active`
requires a recorded certificate, and **no path reaches `active` that does not pass through both** — which
is a CHECK constraint on the table as well as a transition table in PHP, because a transition table only
binds the code that reads it. `failed` is declared and, in this build, **unreachable** — a DNS check that fails leaves the row at
`pending_dns` with a reason, which is what `QRPAGER-14 §6.6` prescribes, so nothing writes `failed`
at all (`R-137`). **`redirecting` is NOT terminal**, and this paragraph said it was until the `§11`
QA review found it disagreeing with `DomainStatus`' own docblock in the same diff: a superseded
hostname keeps answering after a new one goes live, AND a tenant may promote it back, which is
`redirecting -> active`. That move is legal precisely because the row still carries the
`dns_verified_at` and the certificate it earned before.

### 2.4 Global tables — no `tenant_id`, no RLS

A table with no tenant scope column must appear in this list **and** in the allowlist in
`tests/Feature/Database/RlsCoverageTest.php`, or the meta-test fails the build. That is what stops a new
table from quietly escaping tenant isolation.

| Table                   | Columns                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Grants                                     |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ |
| `migrations`            | framework                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | `owner` only                               |
| `users`                 | `id` uuid PK · `name` varchar(120) · `email` varchar(255) **unique**, stored lower-cased · `email_verified_at` timestamptz NULL · `password` varchar(255) NULL _(passkey-only users have none)_ · `remember_token` varchar(100) NULL · `created_at` · `updated_at` · **`is_platform_admin` boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false** _(Task 5)_ · **`two_factor_secret` text NULL** _(Task 5)_ · **`two_factor_recovery_codes` text NULL** _(Task 5)_ · **`two_factor_confirmed_at` timestamptz NULL** _(Task 5)_ | app: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE, **minus the four credential columns on SELECT — `§2.7`, R-006** · worker: SELECT |
| `passkeys` _(Task 5)_ | `id` uuid PK · `user_id` uuid → `users.id` **CASCADE** · `name` varchar(120) · `credential_id` text **unique** · `credential` jsonb default `{}` · `last_used_at` timestamptz NULL · `created_at` · `updated_at` · INDEX `(user_id)` | app: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE `(name, last_used_at, updated_at)`/DELETE · worker: none |
| `personal_access_tokens` _(Task 5)_ | `id` uuid PK · `tokenable_type` varchar(255) · `tokenable_id` uuid · `name` text · `token` varchar(64) **unique** _(the sha256 OF the plaintext)_ · `abilities` text NULL · `last_used_at` timestamptz NULL · `expires_at` timestamptz NULL · `created_at` · `updated_at` · INDEX `(tokenable_type, tokenable_id)` · INDEX `(expires_at)` | app: SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE `(last_used_at, updated_at)`/DELETE · worker: none |
| `password_reset_tokens` | `email` varchar(255) PK · `token` varchar(255) · `created_at`                                                                                                                                                                                                      | app: SELECT/INSERT/DELETE                  |
| `failed_jobs`           | Laravel standard (`id` bigint identity · `uuid` unique · `connection` · `queue` · `payload` · `exception` · `failed_at`)                                                                                                                                           | **worker only**: INSERT/SELECT/DELETE      |

| `tenant_statistics` _(Task 6)_ | `id` uuid PK — **IS the tenant id these aggregates describe** · `sessions_total` · `sessions_waiting` · `sessions_ready` · `sessions_completed` · `sessions_cancelled` · `sessions_expired` · `staff_count` — all integer NOT NULL default 0 CHECK ≥ 0 · `median_wait_seconds` · `p95_wait_seconds` integer NULL CHECK ≥ 0 · `window_start` · `window_end` timestamptz NULL, CHECK ordered · `computed_at` · `created_at` · `updated_at` | app: **SELECT only** · worker: SELECT · INSERT · UPDATE (every aggregate column) |

`users` is global because a user may hold memberships in several tenants and platform staff belong to none.
`failed_jobs` is granted to the worker **only**: a serialized job payload can contain tenant data, and a
global table has no RLS behind it.

**Two tables joined this list at Task 5, and it is the largest single widening of the RLS-free surface since
Task 1.** Stated here rather than implied, because the common justification — *it has to be readable before a
tenant is known* — is true of both and is also exactly the sentence an attacker would like to be true, so it
is the thing a reviewer should push on rather than accept.

- **`passkeys`** — a passkey belongs to a **user**, not to a tenant, and the WebAuthn ceremony identifies the
  user before any tenant is selected. `credential` holds a **public key** and metadata, which is the property
  that makes WebAuthn worth having on this surface: a full database disclosure yields nothing an attacker can
  authenticate with. It is still credential material, so the model marks it `#[Hidden]`.
- **`personal_access_tokens`** — must be resolvable from a bearer token **alone**. Giving it a `tenant_id`
  would make it a tenant table; C4 would then force RLS `ENABLE` + `FORCE` on it; and the row would be
  invisible to the very lookup that has to happen *before* any tenant is known. The only escape is a
  **fifth** named cross-tenant path, which `PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md §4 › Tenancy` forbids without editing
  that file first. **So the tenant a KDS device token is good for travels in `abilities` as `tenant:<uuid>`,
  and it is a CLAIM rather than an authority:** the resolver resolves the tenant from the holder's own
  memberships first and then requires the token's tenant to equal it, so a token naming a tenant its holder
  is not a member of resolves nothing. `token` is the **sha256 of** the plaintext — measured in
  `vendor/laravel/sanctum/src/HasApiTokens.php:66` — so the column is a verifier and not a credential, the
  same posture as `pager_sessions.token_hash`.

**The three vendor migrations are not published, and none of them could be.** Fortify, Sanctum and
`laravel/passkeys` each ship one; read in-session, they use `$table->id()` (bigint, where every id here but
`audit_log`'s is uuid), `$table->timestamp()` (where every timestamp in `§2.5` is `timestamptz`) and
`$table->morphs()` (which would make `tokenable_id` bigint against a uuid `users.id`), and not one of them
grants a column to a role, adds a table to the C4 allowlist, or runs as the owner. The schemas were read and
re-expressed in `2026_10_28_120000_create_auth_contract`.

**And neither package's routes are used.** Installing both with their defaults published **27 unversioned
endpoints outside `/v1`** — `/register`, `/login`, `/logout`, `/forgot-password`, `/two-factor-challenge`,
`/user/passkeys`, Sanctum's `/sanctum/csrf-cookie` and the rest — and `RouteSurfaceTest` rejected the lot,
which is what that test is for. `§6` requires `/v1` and `§11.3` requires every public route to be explicitly
marked and justified, and `/register` is self-service account creation, which this project does not have at
any tier: a staff account comes from Task 6's invite wizard. So `Fortify::$registersRoutes = false`,
`sanctum.routes = false`, and Task 5 mounts what it wants by hand under `/v1`.

**Dropped from the Laravel skeleton:** `sessions`, `cache`, `cache_locks`, `jobs`, `job_batches`. Redis is
the locked store for session, cache and queue (`PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md §1`), so these were five unused
tables, four of which would have needed a tenant-isolation justification they cannot have.

**THREE MORE JOINED AT TASK 6, and they are the largest single widening of the RLS-free surface since
Task 5.** They are **platform** tables under the ruling settled 2026-10-28 (`QRPAGER-13 §0`, rank 1): the
platform admin panel operates only on tables belonging to no tenant, and **a panel query that reaches a
tenant table is a rejected design**. Each holds the platform's own record *about* a restaurant and no tenant
content, which is why there is no scope for RLS to narrow.

- **`tenant_provisionings`** — the provisioning record, and the registry the panel lists (the ruling's
  *"can see that a restaurant exists"*). It is **written before the tenant exists**, which is the one
  property a tenant-scoped table cannot have: at insert time there is no tenant to be scoped to. That is
  also why it carries **no FK** to `tenants.id` — an FK would invert the order and make the failure path, a
  provisioning record for a tenant that was never created, unrepresentable. That record is the only evidence
  a failed attempt leaves.
- **`tenant_statistics`** — one row of aggregates per tenant, written by a job **from inside that tenant's
  own context** and read by the panel from outside. The ruling's *"an aggregate carries no row-level detail:
  no order reference, no token, no session identifier"* is enforced as a property, not a promise:
  `PlatformTableContractTest` pins the column set exactly and asserts none of a forbidden list is in it.
- **`platform_audit_log`** — what a platform admin did to a platform record, append-only by the same
  `ENABLE ALWAYS` statement-level triggers as `audit_log` (`§2.9`). **It exists for a measured reason, not a
  preference:** `audit_log` is a tenant table whose `tenant_id` is nullable and documented in `§2.5` as
  "platform scope", and `tenant_isolation_audit_log` compares `tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid`
  — where `NULL = anything` is `NULL`, never true. Measured at Task 6's Phase 0: the insert is refused
  **`42501` for `qrpager_app` with and without a context, and for `qrpager_owner` without the bypass**, and a
  committed row reads back as **0 rows** for the app role in either state. Only `qrpager_owner` with
  `app.bypass_tenant = 'on'` can write or read one, which is a migration-time posture and not a request-time
  one. **So `§3` row 6's "platform admin actions all land in `audit_log`" was never reachable by a serving
  process at any point in this project's history**; it is met against this table instead, and two docblocks
  asserting the opposite (`User.php`, `RoleMatrix.php`) are corrected in place rather than carried as risks.

**⚠ AND THE THING A REVIEWER SHOULD PUSH ON: none of the three carries a column named `tenant_id`.** That is
deliberate, and it interacts with a live mechanism rather than being cosmetic. C4's meta-test classifies a
table as tenant-scoped by exactly two rules read from `pg_catalog` — `relname = 'tenants'`, or a column named
`tenant_id` — so a platform table carrying that name would be classified tenant-scoped and
`RlsCoverageTest` would demand RLS on it, which the ruling forbids.

**The claim is that it is not a rename to escape the classifier.** Each of these tables is **one row per
tenant**, so the tenant's id is the row's *identity* rather than a scope column over many rows:
`tenant_provisionings.id` **is** the id the tenant will carry, `tenant_statistics.id` **is** the id of the
tenant it describes. That is the exact mirror of the property `§2.5` and `TenantTables` already document for
`tenants` itself — *"its own id IS the tenant scope"* — with the sides reversed: `tenants.id` **scopes**
tenant data, and these ids **reference** a tenant from a record holding none.

**What was rejected.** (a) Naming the column `tenant_id` and giving the tables RLS — then the platform admin,
who holds no tenant context, reads nothing, which is exactly the state Task 5 shipped and Task 6 exists to
fix without widening it. (b) Loosening the meta-test's classifier to a hand-maintained list — that trades the
one mechanical control stopping a *new* tenant table escaping isolation for a label on three tables, which is
the wrong direction.

**So the classifier is owed a replacement, and `tests/Feature/Platform/PlatformTableContractTest.php` is it:**
all three column sets are pinned **exactly** against `information_schema`, so neither a `tenant_id` column
nor a row-level-detail column can join one of these tables without the diff showing it; the three tables are
asserted to carry no RLS *and* to be readable by the app role with `app.tenant_id` unset (the absence of a
policy alone would pass on a table the role had no grant for); and the scope guard's statement matcher is
pinned against all three names, with `audit_log`, `tenants` and `tenant_users` as the controls — because
`platform_audit_log` **embeds** `audit_log` and only survives on the matcher's identifier-boundary lookbehind,
which is a property of a regex rather than of a schema.

### 2.5 Tenant tables — `ENABLE` + `FORCE` RLS on every one (C4)

All timestamps are `timestamptz`. All ids are `uuid` except `audit_log.id`.
"Scope column" is the column every policy compares against `app.tenant_id`.
