**What this task should be remembered for.** Clause 1 of the named invariant failed three times, and
**every failure after the first was introduced by the fix for the one before it.** The first was in
the build; the second was the guard round 1 asked for, refusing one phase after the switch; the
third was the compensation round 2's fix added, deleting one key where the standard is the prefix.
`§11`'s round limit and its scoped-re-review clause are the only reason the third was found rather
than tagged — and the lesson for the next task is the one the third failure makes unmissable: **a
fix to an invariant is new code on the invariant's own path, and it earns a reviewer, not
confidence.**

#### The SECOND scoped re-review — the fourth clause-1 failure, and the ordering that ended it

`§11`'s loop again: a fix to an invariant failure is itself reviewed, scoped to that failure.

**8 findings: 1 Critical, 1 High, 3 Medium, 3 Low — and clause 1 FAILED a fourth time**, by the
step the previous fix had not touched. `manifest.json` was written one step BEFORE the pointer, and
a failed `PUT` of the pointer — or a kill between the two — left the manifest naming a reachable
snapshot with the row at `draft`. No concurrency needed; one failed write. The same two-request
route the task had already declared a clause-1 failure twice, and the class docblock still asserted
the opposite: *"nothing before it is reachable: `{checksum}.html` has a name nobody knows."* It had
a name: the manifest published it.

**This one was not patched. The ORDER changed.**

    assets → snapshot → ROW (guarded) → pointer → manifest

The row commits **before anything becomes reachable**. The snapshot's key is a sha256 of its own
bytes and nothing names it, so a refusal at the guard needs **no compensation at all** — which
matters because the two compensations this method used to carry each caused a clause-1 failure of
their own. The manifest goes last because the manifest is a second pointer.

**That inverts decision D8** — *"the database is the last word"* — and `QRPAGER-14 §0 SR-4` records
the conflict rather than resolving it quietly. D8's ordering fails towards "a page is live that
nothing records"; this one fails towards "a row claims published while the old page still serves".
Only the first is an invariant failure, and `§11` blocks on it.

**The High with it:** the panel rendered Unpublish only when the row said `published`, so in the
state the previous fix existed for — page live, row `draft` — a tenant had no verb. Round 2's
early-return defect, relocated from the service into the view, where the service's own regression
test structurally could not see it. The control is now unconditional.

#### The THIRD scoped re-review — clause 1 a FIFTH time, by the route of the FIRST (2026-10-28)

`§11`'s loop again, scoped to the ordering change (`a8a4edc..4c76ef1`). Past the cap, so only a
failure of the named invariant blocks — and that is what it found.

**10 findings: 1 Critical, 3 High, 4 Medium, 2 Low — and clause 1 FAILED a fifth time**, in the one
step the ordering change had left where it was. `assets → snapshot → ROW → pointer → manifest` puts
the row before everything that NAMES the page, and the section above called that "the row commits
before anything becomes reachable". It was not true of the snapshot: `{checksum}.html` was still
written into `sites/{hostname}/` — the prefix the CDN maps `Host` onto — one step before the commit.

**The argument that failed is the one the previous fix was built on:** *"the snapshot's key is a
sha256 of its own bytes and nothing names it."* `manifest.json` names it, in its body, at a
predictable key, in that same prefix, for the whole life of the publish. And the checksum is a hash
of the document, which `LandingDraftUnreachableTest` already asserts is **stable** across an
unpublish and a re-publish. So the route is four steps and needs no concurrency at all:

1. the page is live; anyone — a crawler, one look — reads `C` from `https://{host}/manifest.json`;
2. the tenant unpublishes: the prefix is emptied, the row says `draft`, and clause 1 holds;
3. any later publish attempt dies between the snapshot write and the commit — the guard refusing,
   `statement_timeout = 5s` or `lock_timeout = 2s` on `qrpager_app`, a worker recycle, a cancelled
   Livewire request;
4. `GET /{C}.html` serves the taken-down page in full, with the row still at `draft`.

The same reviewer pointed at the sentence this repo had deleted in the previous pass — *"'not
reachable' in this project means `allFiles($prefix) === []`; one key's absence was never the
standard"* — and at the test that had been narrowed from the whole prefix to two keys in the same
commit. **A fix pass that rewrites the test to the standard its own change can meet is the shape to
watch for; it is how this one got through the review before.**

**The fix, again an ordering change and not a patch:**

    render + hash (NO NETWORK) → ROW (one keyed statement) → assets → snapshot → pointer → manifest

Rendering never needed the object store: `PublishedSite::assetUrl()` is a pure function of the
private key, so the HTML and its checksum are computable before anything is copied. Phase 2 now
touches neither the database nor the network, and **every store write happens after the row says the
page is published** — which is the only state in which any of those objects is allowed to exist. A
refusal before the commit writes nothing at all, so there is still no compensation on that path.

**The second High is the same clause through a different key** — the asset copies ran in phase 2 too,
and a published asset URL is embedded in the published HTML, so it is public the moment the page is
live. The test that claimed "everything left behind is an unnamed snapshot" published its fixture
with `$mediaId = null`, so the asset-copy loop had never executed inside it. Both are one root and
one fix; they are two entries in the counts.

**The window the fix opened, and what closes it.** With every object write after the commit, an
`unpublish()` landing inside phase 4 empties the prefix and sets the row to `draft`, and the
in-flight publish then writes the pointer into it — clause 1 once more, in the other direction.
Phase 5 reconciles: it re-reads the row, and **when the row says `draft` it sweeps**. That gate is
what makes this the one compensation this method can safely carry — the two it used to have could
fire while the row still said `published`, so each could delete a live page's own objects, and
`draft` is the single state in which nothing of this tenant's may be live at all.

**And the copy stopped being true.** `§12.1`'s "Publish failed — your live page is unchanged" was a
promise the OLD ordering made: every throw site was at or before the pointer write. From the commit
onwards it is false — a failed manifest write leaves the NEW page live, and a failed asset copy
leaves the old page live beside a row that already says `published`. `PublishFailed` now carries its
own headline and `afterRecord()` is the throw for everything from phase 4 on. **The ticket's `§12.1`
copy table is written for the old ordering; `SR-4` carries the consequence** rather than the table
being quietly contradicted by the code.

**Two Mediums were the same defect found a second time.** `R-147` (round 2) and `R-163` (the second
scoped re-review) both recorded the phase-3 guard as a `SELECT`-then-unconditional-`UPDATE`, which
`§4 › Postgres traps` tells this project not to write; `R-163` also mis-stated the window as "two
statements in one transaction" when `TenantContext::run()` wraps **each** `withTenant()` call in its
own transaction, so the guard committed and released before the write began. Phase 3 is now one
statement — `UPDATE … WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status = ? AND published_at IS NOT DISTINCT FROM ?` —
and the affected-row count is checked. **Both rows are CLOSED**, which is the first time a Task 7
row has been closed by a later Task 7 pass rather than deferred.

| Round | Findings | Fixed | Accepted into `§5` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `§11` QA + Security | 29 | 22 | 7 (`R-134`…`R-140`) |
| Fix diff, round 1 | 16 | 13 | 3 (`R-141`…`R-143`) |
| Fix diff, round 2 — the cap | 19 | 5 | 14 (`R-144`…`R-157`) |
| Scoped re-review | 13 | 8 | 5 (`R-158`…`R-162`) |
| Second scoped re-review | 8 | 2 | 6 (`R-163`…`R-168`) |
| Third scoped re-review | 10 | 9 | 1 (`R-170`) |
| **Total** | **95** | **59** | **36** |

`R-169` is in `§5` as well and is deliberately **not** in the column above: it is a residual this
pass's own fix introduced — a publish that has lost its lock can overwrite a newer publish's pointer,
and phase 5 reports it rather than sweeping, because sweeping would take down a page another actor
legitimately published. Counting it as a finding would overstate what the review found; leaving it
out of `§5` would understate what the code now carries. `§5` therefore holds **170** rows while the
findings accepted from six reviews number **36**, and the two figures are different on purpose.

**The honest summary of this task.** Clause 1 failed **five** times. The first was in the build; the
other four were each introduced by, or left in place by, the fix for the one before, and each was
found only because `§11` makes a fix diff reviewable and makes an invariant failure re-reviewable.
Four rounds of patching a race produced three new instances; the fifth was the ordering change being
**almost** right — it moved the row ahead of everything that names the page, and left one object that
a public file had already named. **The lesson the fourth failure taught is confirmed and sharpened by
the fifth: the ordering is the defect, and an ordering is only fixed when nothing reachable is
written before the thing that records it — including the object whose name you believe is a secret.**
The second lesson is narrower and worth as much: **when a fix pass narrows a test's assertion in the
same commit that changes the behaviour, the narrowing is the thing to review.**

#### What this task does NOT deliver — named, with owners

- **No JSON-LD on a published page** (`R-131`, Task 11). The content of a `ld+json`
  element is JSON, so `{{ }}` is the wrong encoder and `{!! !!}` is the only right one —
  and decision D5 says that construct appears nowhere in the template, which a test
  asserts against the source. The meta and Open Graph tags carry the same facts.
- **No per-tenant language on a published page** (`R-132`, Task 11). `lang="en"` and
  `dir="ltr"` are defaults; there is no locale anywhere in the data contract. The CSS is
  written RTL-safe — no physical left/right property, asserted over the stylesheet — so
  the change is two attributes.
- **The platform hostname is not redirected when a custom domain goes live** (`R-133`,
  Task 11). It has no `tenant_domains` row, so nothing demotes it.
- **A certificate becomes `active` when somebody next looks** (`R-130`, Task 13). SR-3.
- **No rich text** (`R-128`, Task 11), which is the cheap half of the invariant: with no
  markup field there is no allow-list to get wrong.
- **Four clauses of `§12`'s accessibility bar are not measured** — a visible focus ring, a
  measured 44 px target, WCAG AA contrast, and `prefers-reduced-motion` actually
  suppressing motion. All four are computed styles and need a browser this machine does
  not have. `R-118`'s scope now covers this panel and the published page as well as Task
  6's. What a server-rendered response does settle is asserted in
  `StudioAccessibilityTest`: one `h1` per page with no skipped level, a label for every
  control, state announced in a live region and never by colour alone, no positive
  `tabindex`, and alt text on every image of a published page.

#### A DEFECT FOUND AFTER THE TAG — the media upload could not work in a browser (2026-10-31)

**Fixed on `fix-studio-upload-endpoint`, branched off `task-7-landing-builder` at `61b220f`.
Not a new `§5` row and not a stop-and-report: it is a defect in what Task 7 shipped, found
while reading `R-116`'s remaining half, and this is the `§4a` record Muhammad's ruling of
2026-10-31 asked for. No new tag — the task's tag stands and this branch carries the fix.**

`RefuseUnservedVendorRoutes` refused `livewire-<8 hex>/upload-file`. That pattern was written
at Task 6 on the argument that **"this panel has no file upload at all"** — true of the
platform panel, and not a sentence that middleware is in a position to say: it is a
**prepended global**, so it refuses a path for every panel this application will ever mount.
Task 7 then shipped `/studio/media`, whose `<input type="file" wire:model="upload">` is
Livewire's ordinary upload path. **So from Task 7's first commit the one validated upload
surface in the product could not receive a file from a browser.**

The chain, every link read in the tree rather than recalled:

| Link | Evidence |
| ---- | -------- |
| the page uses Livewire's uploader | `MediaLibraryPage` has `use WithFileUploads`; the control is `wire:model="upload"` in `resources/views/studio/media.blade.php` |
| which posts to the refused path | `WithFileUploads::_startUpload` takes the `forLocal()` branch unless `FileUploadConfiguration::isUsingS3()`, which reads `config('livewire.temporary_file_upload.disk') ?: config('filesystems.default')` |
| and this installation is on that branch | there is no `config/livewire.php`, and `FILESYSTEM_DISK=local` in both `.env` and `.env.example` |
| so the POST was refused | measured 2026-10-31: **404 `application/problem+json`**, the guard's own document |
| and the suite could not see it | the only driver was `Livewire::test()->set('upload', ...)`, which makes the temporary file IN PROCESS and never issues a request |
| while a test asserted that 404 | `RouteSurfaceTest`'s *"refuses the four vendor routes"* case drove `POST <prefix>/upload-file` and asserted 404 with a problem document |

**The last line is the finding behind the finding.** The guard had a test; the test did not
carry its own copy of the path list (it reads `patterns()` from the guard, which is QA L-2's
fix at Task 7); both were green — because what they agreed on was wrong. **A test that pins a
defect as correct behaviour is the defect**, and `toHaveCount(4)` tells a reader that the list
changed without telling them which way it went.

**The fix, in one commit:**

- `upload-file` removed from `REFUSED`. **`preview-file` STAYS refused** — nothing in this
  application calls `temporaryUrl()` and the media view renders no preview — which is
  narrower than `R-116`'s instruction, that said to remove both.
- `RouteSurfaceTest` now asserts that path is **SERVED**: an unsigned POST answers **401**,
  from Livewire's own `abort_unless(request()->hasValidRelativeSignature(), 401)`, and the
  path matches no pattern in `patterns()`. Three refusals and one positive, rather than a
  count.
- **`StudioMediaUploadTest` (new) crosses the endpoint over HTTP** — the signed URL the
  component really hands the browser, a multipart POST, the signed path back, `_finishUpload`
  the way the browser calls it, `store()`, and the PNG's own sha256 read back off the object
  store. Measured red before the fix (`404 != 200`), green after.
- **NOT `FILESYSTEM_DISK=s3`**, which would have made the 404 disappear by having the browser
  PUT raw bytes into the bucket before `InspectedImage` ever read them — the one thing
  `MediaLibraryPage`'s docblock says that page exists to prevent. The first case asserts
  `isUsingS3()` is false for exactly that reason, so the bypass fails a test rather than
  passing quietly.

**One thing recorded rather than closed.** Livewire's default temporary-upload rule is
`max:12288` (12 MB) and no `config/livewire.php` narrows it, while `InspectedImage::MAX_BYTES`
is 5 MB and `media_assets_size_is_bounded` is the same number. So a **signed** caller can make
the application write up to 12 MB to its temporary disk for a file the library will then
refuse. The third case pins that asymmetry deliberately rather than leaving it unstated;
narrowing a vendor's rules is a sizing decision and belongs with `R-122`/`R-123`'s pass at
Task 12.

#### THE SAME GAP ONE SURFACE OVER, closed 2026-10-31 — the update endpoint, and the ranges that hid it

**The sweep Muhammad ordered after the row above found no second row that was secretly a
defect. It found something worse-placed: the endpoint through which EVERY write in both
panels travels had no functional test at all, and the assertions that did touch it were
satisfied by the very refusal they should have caught.**

`POST /livewire-<hash>/update` carries save, publish, unpublish, upload, delete, add a
domain, advance a domain, and every table search, sort and modal submit in `/platform`.
Before today:

| What drove it | What that proved |
| ------------- | ---------------- |
| ~20 action cases, via `Livewire::test()` | nothing about HTTP: the helper calls the component in process |
| `StudioPanelInvariantTest` | nothing at all — `studioRoutes()` scanned `/studio` and the endpoint is not under it |
| `PlatformPanelInvariantTest`, as a platform admin | `toBeLessThan(500)` — **a 404 passes** |
| `PlatformPanelInvariantTest`, anonymously | `>= 300 and < 500` — **a 404 passes** |
| `PlatformPanelInvariantTest`, as each tenant principal | `>= 400 and < 500` — **a 404 passes** |

So a global middleware refusing that path would have left both panels unable to do
anything, with 1088 tests green. That is `R-116` exactly, on a path forty times more
load-bearing than the one it hid.

**⚠ AND THE OBVIOUS PROBE DOES NOT WORK, which is the finding inside the finding.** Two
measurements, 2026-10-31:

- a bare `POST <prefix>/update` answers **404 from Livewire itself** —
  `RequireLivewireHeaders` aborts 404 with no `X-Livewire` header (*"to avoid confirming the
  endpoint exists to scanners"*, in the vendor's own comment) and `handleUpdate()` aborts
  404 again on an empty payload. **The endpoint's own refusal and a guard's refusal are the
  same status**, so no bare-POST assertion of any value can tell them apart.
- **419 is not available to a test at all**: `VerifyCsrfToken` skips itself when
  `runningUnitTests()`. The 419 a browser gets, and that `§4a` quotes from the `local`
  environment above, cannot be observed from inside the suite.

**So the only honest proof is a real update**, and `Tests\Support\LivewireRequest` builds
one the way the browser does: GET the page, read the `wire:snapshot` the server embedded in
it, post it back with a call on it. Both panels now have a case that does exactly that:

- **studio**: an owner's `$refresh` answers **200** and its `effects.html` carries the
  media library's own row (`owner-can-see-this.png`).
- **platform**: an admin's `$refresh` answers **200** and carries the registry row inserted
  a moment earlier.
- **and the snapshot is not a bearer token**: replayed by another tenant's staff, by a
  platform admin, by a tenant owner against the platform page, and anonymously, it answers
  **403 with an empty `effects.html`** every time, and a replayed `delete` deletes nothing.
  That is Task 6's security M-1 asked over HTTP rather than through `canAccess()`, and it
  holds.

**TWO MISTAKES THIS WORK MADE AND CAUGHT, both recorded because `§4a` is where they go.**
*(1)* The first version of the probe took **the first `wire:snapshot` in the page**, which
is `Filament\Livewire\Topbar` — a Filament page mounts four components — and reached a
conclusion about a component that re-renders for anybody because it holds no tenant
content. It reported "anonymous replay → 200" and, read naively, that was a Critical that
does not exist. `LivewireRequest::snapshotFor()` therefore takes the component BY NAME, and
every positive case asserts a needle rather than a status alone. *(2)* The control for that
needle was written as `->toContain($needle, $message)` — and Pest's matcher is **variadic**,
so the message became a second needle and the case failed for its own text. Guard rule 7
refuses that form; this is the second time it has earned its place.

**THE RANGES, SWEPT AND TIGHTENED.** An inequality is the vacuous-assertion family with a
different face, so every status assertion in the suite was read. Four were replaced with
the exact value, measured one principal per case (the first measurement reused a session
across principals and produced a different, wrong matrix — recorded because it would have
been pinned as truth):

| Where | Was | Now |
| ----- | --- | --- |
| `PlatformPanelInvariantTest`, admin / anonymous / tenant principals | `< 500`, `>= 300 < 500`, `>= 400 < 500` | an exact table: 200 / 302, 401, 403, and the update endpoint's own 404 named as NOT an authorization refusal |
| `StudioPanelInvariantTest`, four cases | `->not->toBe(200)` | the same exact table per principal, logout included rather than skipped |
| `LandingDraftUnreachableTest`, two cases | `->not->toBe(200)` | **401** anonymous, **403** staff and platform admin — the distinction the inequality erased |
| `ProblemRetryAfterTest` | `< 500` for three SQLSTATEs | **409**, **422**, **403** per state. ⚠ The row-writer guessed 404 for `42501` and the exact assertion caught it immediately, which is the argument for exact values in one line |
| `PanelRateLimitTest` | `429 count >= 1` | **exactly 2**, which is what `$limit + 2` requests means |

Deliberately left as ranges, with the reason: `toBeIn([200, 503])` on `/readyz` in three
files (readiness is live state and the case asserts it answered at all), and
`RestaurantCreateActionTest`'s `strlen($refused) < 1000` (its own comment explains that
Livewire's harness turns `abort(403)` into a near-empty render, so there is no status to
assert — those two cases are the remaining in-process drivers, and `LivewireRequest` now
makes an exact-403 HTTP version of them possible if Muhammad wants it). Every other
inequality in the suite is over a count, a TTL, a duration or a saturation fraction, where
a range is the honest form.

**And `R-122` is one path narrower than it was:** three refused vendor paths are unmetered
404s, not four. The upload endpoint is served, and it is metered twice over — Livewire's own
`throttle:60,1`, and `RateLimit:panel` (240/min per IP, 600/min per tenant), because
`bootstrap/app.php` appends that bucket to the `web` group and this route is in it. So the path
did not move from unmetered-refusal to unmetered-service.

**Measured in the `local` environment, not only under the harness** (the suite disables CSRF, so
it cannot see this): `POST <prefix>/upload-file` → **419** from `VerifyCsrfToken`, i.e. served
and asking for the token Livewire's JS sends; `POST <prefix>/update` → 419, unchanged;
`GET <prefix>/preview-file/x` and `GET /filament/exports/1/download` → **404**, still refused.

#### The `§5.1` invariant — both clauses, and the second is an UNREACHABILITY proof

`§5.1`: *no component carries a hard-coded colour, spacing or font size, and no tenant-supplied theme
value can reach the order-ready screen's colour pair.* `QRPAGER-15 §5.1` is explicit that the second
half is **unreachability, not a clamp** — and **there is no clamp anywhere in the task**, asserted by
a scan over every file in the path.

The mechanism in one sentence: `ThemeTokens::NAMES` is a **closed allow-list of twelve**,
`ThemeTokens::property()` maps a name to a CSS custom property by a pure string transform, and the
three properties the order-ready screen reads are **outside the image of that function over that
list**. Five independent assertions carry it — disjointness computed from the PHP source **parsed**
rather than copied (guard rule 11c's own argument), every one of the twelve names pushed through the
real transform, each protected property declared **exactly once and in neither theme block**, hostile
values for all twelve plus three forged `--ready-*` names applied to the ancestor exactly as the
publish pipeline does, and the no-clamp scan.

#### `R-118` — 8a's share is CLOSED; the panel's share is 8b's

The four clauses, each measured in Chromium 156.0.8078.4 (chromium build v1248) rather than asserted:
a **2px** computed outline on six controls with the ring proven distinguishable from its surroundings,
every interactive box **≥ 44px on both axes** from the engine's own layout, AAA and AA pairs resolved
by the engine in **both** themes, 1.4.11's **3:1** on the input border, and `prefers-reduced-motion`
resolving to **exactly 0ms** with the spinner's animation removed outright — with a positive control
asserting **160ms** without the preference, so a zero cannot come from a stylesheet that never loaded.

`R-118` **stays open with its share reduced, not closed**: its own resolution requires the figures be
taken *"against the token-styled panel, not the default one"*, and the panel is restyled in
`QRPAGER-23`.

#### Eight defects the task's own tests caught before any reviewer

Each fixed at the SHAPE rather than the symptom, which is what `QRPAGER-15 §8` requires of a repeat:

1. **The order-ready colours were theme ROLES**, so *"identical in both themes"* was false for two of
   the three — `paper` resolves to `#F2F4F1` in light and `#0A1F17` in dark. Redesigned into a
   `--ready-*` namespace emitted **exactly once**, outside both theme blocks.
2. **The lint rule laundered a literal:** `padding: var(--space-16) 9px` passed, because the value
   check early-returned on *"contains a `var()`"*. The **bad** fixture predicted the line and the rule
   did not produce it.
3. **Its shorthand splitter could not see nesting** — a regex lookahead — so `clamp(a, b, c)` was torn
   into fragments and each rejected. Found by the **good** fixture, which is the half that stops a rule
   being disabled for crying wolf.
4. **It accepted `color: 'white'`** in an inline style object: no hex, no colour function, no digit.
   Colour now has its own allow-list judgement.
5. **The CSS scanner walked into `node_modules`** and reported **69** findings in jsdom's own
   stylesheet, because its exemptions matched root-relative prefixes only and pnpm with `hoist=false`
   puts a `node_modules` in every package.
6. **`focusableWithin` filtered on `offsetParent` and `getClientRects`**, so without a layout engine
   the focus trap trapped **nothing** — the exact failure a focus trap exists to prevent, by the back
   door. The probe is gone; the trap asks the DOM instead.
7. **The first font fetch shipped 27 KB twice.** Plus Jakarta Sans is a variable font and Google serves
   one file for both weights.
8. **One browser check could never have passed:** *"no element sets `outline: none`"* describes every
   unfocused element in Chromium, since `outline-style` initialises to `none` while `outline-width`
   initialises to `medium`. It reported the whole document. Replaced, with the source-level half moved
   to a scan that can fail.

#### Clause 1 of the named invariant fell a SECOND time, so `§8` required the redesign

**SEC M-1.** The lint rule cannot see Tailwind's **default palette and scales**, which are
live in both apps. Measured: `text-[#fff]` and `p-[13px]` exit 1, but **`bg-red-500 p-4
text-sm` gives `lint:es` 0 and `lint:tokens` 0.** There is no `@theme` block anywhere, so
`@import 'tailwindcss'` leaves the full default theme reachable — including `--text-sm` at
**14px**, which is not on the approved type scale at all.

That is the second fall. The first was the laundered `var(--space-16) 9px` earlier this
round. `QRPAGER-15 §8`: *if a clause of the named invariant falls a second time, the second
fix is not a patch on the state that was found — it is a redesign that makes the whole shape
impossible.* A pattern rejecting default-theme-backed utilities would be the patch, and would
also be a **second source for Tailwind's default theme**: every colour, step and size it
ships, listed by hand, stale at the next minor version.

**`packages/tokens/generated/theme.css`** is a generated `@theme reference` block that
**clears** each namespace (`--color-*: initial`) and repopulates it from the token source, so
`bg-red-500`, `p-5` and `text-sm` **compile to nothing** — there is no utility to write.

**`reference` rather than plain `@theme`, and the modifier is load-bearing.** Plain `@theme`
emits every variable into `:root`, which would be a **second declaration** of `--color-paper`
beside `generated/tokens.css`'s AND would break the dark theme, because a `:root` declaration
Tailwind emitted would not follow `[data-theme='dark']`. Under `reference` nothing is emitted
and each utility resolves `var(--color-paper, var(--color-paper))`, so the value comes from
`tokens.css` and the attribute still decides it. **Every entry is a `var()` reference and no
literal appears in the file.**

**Proven on fixtures, both directions, against the REAL `apps/web/app/globals.css` through
Tailwind 4.3.3's own compiler:** the bad fixture's 17 default-theme utilities emit **nothing**,
and the good fixture's token-backed ones all emit with a `var()` value — the half that stops
*"nothing is emitted for `bg-red-500`"* being true for the uninteresting reason. With the
`@theme` import removed, **15** of the bad fixture's classes compile again.

Two decisions inside it worth stating. **`--tracking-*` and `--leading-*` are cleared and NOT
repopulated**: the approved set carries no letter-spacing and no line-height token, so every
value Tailwind ships for them is a decision nobody approved — `tracking-wide` was the one
default utility that survived the block's first version, found by the bad fixture rather than
by reading it. And **`p-4` is deliberately not in the bad fixture**: under the token theme it
is `var(--space-4)`, an approved step. The trap is written into the fixture's header instead —
**the spacing scale is named in PX, so `p-4` is 4px here and was 16px under Tailwind's default
multiplier.** The utility is legitimate; the number means something different.

#### `mailto:` — the stored address could open the URI's header section

**SEC L-2.** The href interpolated the tenant-supplied address raw.
`FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL` accepts a **quoted local part** — measured on this repository's PHP
8.4, `"?subject=hi&body=click"@c.d` passes Task 7's validator and is stored — and the first
unencoded `?` ends the address and opens the header section, so a mail client composes with a
**tenant-chosen subject and body**. No XSS; the attribute is HTML-escaped.

**Percent-encoded per RFC 6068, not `encodeURIComponent`.** RFC 6068's `some-delims` keeps
`! $ ' ( ) * + , ; : @` literal, so `@` and `+` survive — `encodeURIComponent` would encode
`@` and break every address. `,` is encoded deliberately: RFC 6068 uses it to separate
addresses and this renders one. Iterated by **code point**, so an astral character is one
character. Five cases, including the exact measured address **and the DOM it renders into**,
because a correct helper that is unused is the same vacuity one level up.

**The `tel:` sibling has reasoned about this class since Task 7** — its validator refuses `,`
and `;` because a `tel:` URI reads them as a dial pause and a parameter separator. The email
field got none of that reasoning, which is the asymmetry this closes.

of how visible a comment is as a control. `composer contracts:check` was step seven of
`apps/api/bin/gate` and a step of **no** CI job, while the comment at the frontend job's
`tokens:check` said it was *"in the `gates` job above"*.

The step is added and the false comment is corrected **where it stands**, saying it was false
rather than quietly rewording. The mechanical half: `ci-parity.test.mjs` was scoped to the
**frontend** job, so nothing caught the PHP gate drifting. It covers `apps/api/bin/gate`
against the `gates` job in both directions now, reading each side's own list — the
`steps=(…)` array and the `composer …` run lines — with `PHP_CI_ONLY` naming the provisioning
steps and the coverage run explicitly, so a new CI-only step has to be justified there.
A fifth case asserts every composer script both sides name exists in `composer.json`: a step
list is only as good as the scripts behind it. **Proven both ways.**

#### The coverage denominator was wrong, so the number was never about this task

**QA #10.** `96.73%` was measured over `packages/tokens/src`, `packages/ui/src` and
`tools/design-tokens/*.mjs`, which left about **990 lines of this task's own code** out of the
denominator: `generate.mjs` (620), `fetch-fonts.mjs` (241), `bin/scan-css.mjs` (129). `§6`
asks for coverage *on code this task added*, so the figure was never about that set.

**Re-measured over the whole of it, the honest number was 59.44 / 70.37 / 60.84 / 60.03** —
the three were essentially uncovered, and reporting that alone would have been a gate clause
nobody met. So they are **covered**, and not by line-count tests: each builder is asserted
against the SOURCE's own computation, `buildTs`'s output is handed to `tsc`, `buildPhp`'s to
`php -l` **and** to `php -r 'require'` so the round trip is through the consumer Laravel's
config loader will be, and `run()` returns a status instead of calling `process.exit`, which
is what lets check mode, the stale-diff branch, the missing-file branch and the writer all run
in-process.

**`fetch-fonts.mjs` was also UNIMPORTABLE:** a bare top-level `await main()` meant importing
it fetched from `fonts.googleapis.com` and wrote into the package, so nothing in it could be
covered at all. The entry point is guarded and the pure half — parse, deduplicate, name, emit
— is exported and tested against a **committed css2 response**. The network half is not
unit-tested and is not pretended to be.

**⚠ AND THAT FOUND A REAL DEFECT:** Prettier had reformatted `fonts.css`, rewrapping every
`unicode-range`, so **the committed file was not what the generator emits**. Nothing caught
it, because the fetch script needs the network and is therefore not a gate step, so there is
no byte diff to go red. `packages/tokens/fonts/` is in `.prettierignore` now — the same rule
the other generated artefacts already had — and both font artefacts are asserted
byte-identical to their builders.

**The final figure, over the honest denominator: 92.18% statements · 90.67% branches ·
98.23% functions · 93.05% lines.** `tools/gate/bin/*` stays out with the reason stated rather
than implicit: `gate.mjs` exports no unit and covering it means running the gate inside its
own coverage pass, and its step list is asserted by the parity test in both directions
against both halves of CI — a stronger claim than a line count. The shell scripts v8 cannot
instrument at all.

#### To `§5` with an owner and a date — one row

**SEC L-3 → `R-171`.** `apps/web` and `apps/site` ship with `poweredByHeader: false` and no
`headers()`: no CSP, no `nosniff`, no `Referrer-Policy`, no `X-Frame-Options`, no
`Permissions-Policy`, on either origin, and no `§5` row, no gate clause and no out-of-scope
line. It matters because of **which** origin: `§3` row 9(b) requires `apps/site` to load no
third-party script, and Task 3 puts the raw QR token in the **URL fragment**, where any script
on that origin reads `location.hash`. **Measured:** both apps are statically prerendered with
no route handler, middleware or server action, so the headers land **at the edge** — Task 13's
surface, `R-135`'s precedent, with Task 12 owning the CSP's content. **Not built here**, and
the reason is `§8` rather than scope: the clause these headers satisfy is *a captured response
carries them*, and there is no deployed environment to capture one from, so a `headers()` block
committed now would be a control nobody could assert against. The row names **both** origins,
**Task 13 (`QRPAGER-20`)** for the mechanism and **Task 12 (`QRPAGER-19`)** for the content,
review-by **2026-12-06** — the same date as `R-135`, because splitting them would let one be
fixed and the other forgotten.

#### FOUR DEFECTS THIS ROUND'S OWN GATE AND EVIDENCE FOUND, after the 24 findings

None came from a reviewer. All four are recorded because each is a shape this project has
named before, and three of them were in the machinery that writes evidence — which is where
a defect is most expensive, because it makes a green verdict unreliable rather than wrong.

**1 · A fixture email built from a UUID's TIMESTAMP collided 198 times in 200.** The PHP
gate reported **15 failed / 1084 passed**, and every failure carried ONE identity:
`users_email_unique` on `acting-01a1932b11bf@example.test`. **That prefix decodes to
18:13:55.775 — it IS a millisecond timestamp.** Nineteen call sites across eleven test files
built a *"unique"* address as `substr(str_replace('-', '', $uuid), 0, 12)`, and a v7 UUID's
first 48 bits are the millisecond timestamp while twelve hex characters are exactly those 48
bits. **ramsey/uuid's v7 is MONOTONIC:** inside one millisecond it keeps the timestamp and
increments a counter in the tail, so two UUIDs made in the same millisecond share those
twelve characters **exactly**. Measured: 200 consecutive `Str::uuid7()` calls through that
expression gave **2 distinct emails and 198 collisions**. It survived Tasks 5, 6 and 7
because each test takes about 0.2s, so consecutive fixtures usually landed in different
milliseconds; bunch them and the constraint raises 23505.
**Fixed at all 19 sites — the WHOLE uuid**, so uniqueness rests on the UUID's own uniqueness
and not on where its entropy sits. Taking the LAST twelve would also have worked and is
rejected deliberately: it would rest on ramsey's counter living in the tail, which is an
implementation detail this repository has no business depending on. `TestFixtureUniquenessTest`
asserts the **property**, with the truncated form asserted to collide from the same loop so
the case records the defect as well as the fix, plus a scan over every test file because a
new file copying the expression from a neighbour is how it reached nineteen.
**`R-049`'s argument is that an unidentified flake is the most expensive defect shape on this
branch, so this one is identified by mechanism and gets a test rather than a row.** It is NOT
`R-092`'s claim-shortfall family, and `QRPAGER-15 §0.1`'s working rule for this branch is
that every other red blocks. ⚠ *And the scan flagged itself on its first run — its pattern
lives in a double-quoted string, which comment-stripping does not reach. That is the FOURTH
instance in this task of a check reading its own text as evidence.*

**2 · The shell checker's performance assertion flaked at 34,225 ms.** Its own comment said
the 3000 ms bound was 60× the measured 0.048 s *"so it cannot flake on a loaded runner"*.
Measured three times immediately afterwards on the same machine: **0.05 s each**. The 34 s
run was concurrent with `composer gate`'s `php artisan test`. **Wall clock on a shared
machine is not a measurement of the code**, which is `F10`'s shape one level over — that row
records *"a loaded host turned a passing timeout proof into a red at 27.6 s"*.
**The bound is NOT raised, and that is the point:** a per-line subprocess loop measured
4.35 s locally and 6.67 s on a runner, so a bound generous enough to absorb 34 s would PASS
the regression and the assertion would mean nothing. What changed is the **statistic** —
three runs, fastest judged, all three reported in the failure message so a future red says
whether it was the code or the host.

**3 · The script writing the frontend gate's transcript hit the `$?` hazard this task
mechanised.** It put an `echo` between `pnpm gate` and the read, so the transcript said
*"exit code, read DIRECTLY: 0"* for a run that had exited 1 — in the file that is
`check-shell-evidence`'s own evidence. The read is on the line after the command now and the
transcript states which form it used rather than claiming directness. `check-shell-evidence`
scans executable scripts in the repository and this one lived in a scratch directory, which
is exactly the gap: the rule is mechanised for committed scripts and not for the hand that
writes a transcript.

**4 · The `.gitignore` guard's own non-vacuity floor counted BUILD OUTPUTS.** It asserted
`examined >= 4`, where `examined` counts nested directories matching an unanchored pattern —
in this working tree `apps/api/build`, both apps' `.next` and four `node_modules`, **none of
which is tracked**. A fresh clone has no `build/` and no `.next/`, so the walk found 3 and
the fresh-clone proof went red. **A test that depended on the builder's machine having run a
build, inside the one suite the fresh-clone proof exists to protect** — `§6` verbatim: *"a
pass that depends on something only present on the builder's machine is not a pass."* The
floor is about the WALKER now and proves itself against `packages/ui/src/styles`, which is
tracked, nested and not optional. Zero candidates in a fresh clone is a real and correct
state, so the count is reported rather than bounded.


The stripped line read `#151, ...`. The figure survives in that object only because a *later*
occurrence of it is indented, so its `#` is not first on the line. **Reproduced rather than
inferred**, in a throwaway repository: the same file tagged with the default cleanup drops the
line; with `--cleanup=verbatim` it keeps it. `task-8a` is **not** re-tagged over a message
defect — the tag is the delivery record and moving it to fix prose would be worse than the

#### 3 · THE SUITE'S REDS ARE ATTRIBUTABLE NOW — the item that protects every later task

**`R-200` is FIXED, and its own row named the wrong mechanism.** The row says the harness's
seeded session is removed by *"a concurrent test's `TRUNCATE`"*. It cannot be:
`bin/poll-latency-proof` has run on its own database since it was written
(`qrpager_poll_proof`) and the suite runs on `qrpager_test` (`phpunit.xml:64`), so **no
statement the suite issues can reach a row that harness wrote.** Postgres was never the shared
resource. **Redis was**, and Redis is shared by every Postgres database: a pager session IS a
Redis key (`§4 › Realtime` makes the token pointer's own name the secret), and
`TestCase::setUp` calls `clearPagerProjection()` before **every** test, deleting
`t:*:pager:*` and `pager:tok:*`. With one prefix and one logical database for both processes
those patterns matched the keys the harness had just seeded — hence a 404 on a poll, and hence
9-in-20 rather than always, because it takes one test boundary landing inside one batch.

**Measured both ways, and the reproduction is deterministic rather than statistical:** a loop
deleting `*pager*` from Redis while the harness runs — exactly what `setUp` does, with no
Postgres and no load in the path — failed **10 of 10**; with the fix in place, **0 of 10**.

The fix is a keyspace of its own: `REDIS_DB`, `REDIS_CACHE_DB` and `REDIS_PREFIX` set before
the framework boots, the same mechanism the script already used for `DB_DATABASE`. ⚠ **Neither
candidate the row proposed would have worked.** *"Give the subprocess its own database"* is
already true and is not the axis that matters; and *"have the harness take `R-049`'s lock"*
**deadlocks** — the suite holds that lock for its whole process lifetime and is blocked
waiting on the subprocess, so a subprocess waiting on the lock waits for ever.

⚠ **AND THE REVERT PROOF CAUGHT A DEFECT IN THE FIX'S OWN CODE.** `getenv(...) ?: '3'` returns
`'3'` for a deliberate `POLL_PROOF_REDIS_DB=0`, because `'0'` is falsy in PHP — so the first
attempt at the revert proof passed the logical-database assertion and reddened one line
further down, which reads as *the fix working* when it was *the override being ignored*. Each
variable is now false-tested. Found by the proof, not by reading.

**THE NAMED KNOWN-FLAKE LIST.** `apps/api/tests/known-flakes.json`, with `bin/classify-reds`
doing the split and `bin/gate` reporting it **separately from failures** — and printing the
list at the top of **every** run, green or red, so a stale entry is visible to whoever reads
the log. Verdict in the exit code: **0** no failures · **1** at least one failure on no row,
a REAL red and the gate's own failure · **2** every failure attributed to a named row.
**Exit 2 is deliberately not 0:** a regression in any file on the list would look exactly like
an attributed red, and making it green would remove the reading `R-191`'s and `R-172`'s owner

⚠ **THERE ARE TWO SYMPTOM FAMILIES, NOT THE THREE ROWS THE SWEEP WAS FRAMED AROUND**, and the

#### ⚠ FOUR DEFECTS IN THIS TASK'S OWN CODE, FOUND BY ITS OWN TESTS AND BY ITS OWN REVERT PROOF

Recorded because each is the shape this project keeps paying for, and because three of the four
would have shipped silently.

1. **`apps/web/tsconfig.json` DID NOT INCLUDE `src`, SO THE TYPECHECK WAS VACUOUS.**
   `pnpm typecheck` reported success over ~1,400 lines it had not read. This is 8a's QA finding
   one level down — *"`pnpm run typecheck` skipped the root TS project, so a planted TS2345 in
   the 708-line browser suite passed typecheck AND lint"* — and the fix is the same: the
   project includes the code it claims to check.
2. **The iOS install flow was hidden on `alerts.unsupported`, which is the state an iOS TAB
   LANDS IN.** Apple exposes `Notification` and `PushManager` only to a web app launched from
   the Home Screen, so an iPhone reading the page in Safari has no push path at all, reports
   `unsupported`, and was the one customer shown no install instructions — while
   `§4 › Realtime` calls that guidance *"a required product path, not a nice-to-have"* and the
   install is the only thing that would fix their state.
3. **The reconcile registered a push device for a session already known to be over, and before
   the session was resolved at all.** Both are refused server-side by design, so nothing broke;
   what happened instead is a request that can only fail, on every launch of a finished
   session. ⚠ **And the terminal guard was covered by NOTHING** — `bin/revert-proof` found
   that, because removing both guards left the expired case green: that case is caught by the
   snapshot guard, and a `completed` session HAS a snapshot.
4. **Two negative assertions waited on a fixed 50 ms sleep.** One passed, then failed when an
   unrelated case was added to the same file, then passed again when its failure MESSAGE grew.
   `reconcileSubscription()` calls `getSubscription()` before it decides anything, so the test
   container counts those and both assertions wait for the decision rather than for a duration.

#### ⚠ AND FOUR IN THE HARNESS ITSELF, each measured rather than reasoned

The browser toolchain is new to this repository, and every one of these was a red suite with a
cause that was not the code.

1. **`--network host` does not reach the host's loopback on this platform.** 300-ish: measured
   as `000` from a container against a server answering **200** through
   `--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway`. And `localhost` cannot be borrowed: Docker
   appends `--add-host` AFTER the default `127.0.0.1 localhost`, so the container's own loopback
   wins — measured, both entries present in `/etc/hosts`.
2. **`host.docker.internal` is on no engine's secure-origin allow-list**, so
   `navigator.serviceWorker` and `navigator.credentials` are both `undefined` over http. The
   whole service-worker half of this task was unreachable until a TLS front existed:
   chromium answered *"Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'register')"* and firefox
   *"navigator.serviceWorker is undefined"*.
3. **The teardown leaked `next-server`.** `kill` on a launcher subshell leaves the server; and
   `setsid` plus `kill -- -PGID` fixes three of four, because `next start` spawns `next-server`
   in a process group of its own. The visible cost: one run found port 3099 held, its readiness
   probe passed against the STALE server — which was serving the previous build's asset
   manifest against a `.next` rebuilt underneath it — and **33 of 45 journey cases failed with
   `400 Bad Request` on every JS chunk**, against bytes nobody built in that run.
4. **`pnpm exec` re-linked `node_modules` mid-run** (`+ vite 8.3.5 / + vitest 5.0.5 /
   Done in 1.1s`), after which `pnpm exec playwright` failed with *"Command not found"* against
   a tree that was correct a second later. `npm_config_verify_deps_before_run=false` did not
   stop it; the pinned binaries are invoked directly now. A run that mutates its own toolchain
   cannot be measured.

#### ⚠ AND TWO MORE, NEITHER FOUND BY A TEST THIS TASK WROTE

**1. `StatusMirrorContractTest` — AN INHERITED GUARD — CAUGHT TWO SECOND DECLARATIONS OF THE
STATUS ENUM IN THIS TASK'S OWN CODE.** `composer gate` at `fcdfd8f` went red at step **10 of
10**, the nine before it green, on *"it writes no second DECLARATION of a status list outside
the generated mirror"*, naming `apps/web/src/pager/journey.ts` and
`apps/web/src/screens/SessionEnded.tsx`. `bin/classify-reds` put it on no `known-flakes.json`
row: **REAL RED, 1 of 1**, `Tests: 1 failed, 1166 passed (9913 assertions)`.

It was right both times, and the second one is the interesting one:

- `journey.ts` declared the six screen prefixes as a hand-written union, and two of those
  prefixes — `waiting`, `ready` — are spelled exactly like two of the five `pager_status`
  values. One declaration carrying two status words is what `§6.2` forbids, and the guard
  cannot tell it from a copy of the enum because from outside the file it is not
  distinguishable from one.
- `SessionEnded.tsx` declared its three states as a union of the enum's three **terminal**
  statuses, and keyed two copy maps by them.

**Neither is fixed by exempting it, and the fix is the better artefact anyway**: `PrefixOf` and
`SuffixOf` take the two halves of a `ScreenState` with a template-literal `infer`, so `Screen`
and all six per-screen state unions now come OUT of `JOURNEY_STATES` and cannot drift from it —
where the old lists merely agreed with it on the day they were written. `SessionEnded` builds
its copy keys by template, so the compiler checking ``` `ended.${EndedState}.title` ``` against
`CopyKey` is what requires copy for every terminal status; measured before being relied on (the
good form typechecks, `ended.nope.title` is a `TS2345`). `TERMINAL` is now derived from
`PAGER_STATUS_TRANSITIONS` — an empty transition list IS what terminal means — rather than
listed; the guard did not flag that one, and it is the same defect class.

⚠ **THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THE COMMENT EXPLAINING THE FIX LEFT THE FILE RED.** The guard reads
raw source, comments included, so quoting the rejected line re-created the offence inside the
comment about it. It is described there now, not quoted — and that is recorded in the comment
itself, because the next person to explain a guard in a comment will reach for the quote.

**2. `pnpm gate` COULD NOT BE RUN ON THIS HOST AT ALL, and the tests were fine.** Step 11 died
for all five Playwright projects with

```
chrome-headless-shell: error while loading shared libraries: libnspr4.so
```

`test:browser` invoked `playwright test` directly, `playwright install-deps` needs root, and
this builder has no sudo — so the workspace gate was **unrunnable**, which is the same defect
`apps/api/bin/gate`'s `PAO_DISABLE=1` exists for one half over: *a gate whose result depends on
which machine runs it is not a gate.* `test:browser` now goes through
`tools/browsers/bin/browsers`, which probes the host, execs **natively** when all three engines
launch — which they do on CI, where the `frontend` job installs them, so this costs CI nothing
— and uses the pinned image when they do not. It also pins `node_modules/.bin/playwright`
rather than `pnpm exec`, because pnpm 12 relinks `node_modules` before running a script and did
so mid-run. A new `ci-parity` case fails on any `package.json` script that runs
`playwright test` without the runner, and asserts there IS one so the filter is not vacuous.

**3. ⛔ A TASK 5 GRANT MADE EVERY PASSKEY LOGIN RETURN `403`, AND 1,167 TESTS COULD NOT SEE IT.**
`browser/passkey.spec.ts` — a virtual authenticator over CDP against the real API — got
`passkey login -> 403` where it wanted 200. The API's own log named it:

```
SQLSTATE[42501]: Insufficient privilege: permission denied for table passkeys
```

`2026_10_28_120000_create_auth_contract.php` granted `UPDATE (name, last_used_at, updated_at)
ON passkeys`, and `Laravel\Passkeys\Actions\VerifyPasskey::updatePasskey()` writes **`credential`**
and `last_used_at` after every successful assertion. `credential` is not in that list, so the
UPDATE raised `42501` and `DatabaseErrorMapper` mapped it to `ProblemType::Forbidden`.
Registration succeeded; login never could.

⚠ **AND THE COLUMN IS NOT COSMETIC.** The vendor's own comment on that method: *"The credential
must be persisted after each use to store the updated signature counter, which is used to detect
cloned authenticators."* So the missing grant also froze WebAuthn's clone-detection counter at
its registration value for the lifetime of every key.

⚠ **HOW IT SURVIVED THE SUITE, measured rather than assumed:** nothing drives the assertion
ceremony as `qrpager_app`, because the counter is written only after a real authenticator signs a
real challenge. Checked that this was not merely a stale development database — `qrpager_test`
carries the **identical** column grants. `R-100` is the `§5` row that asked for this toolchain,
and the harness found this on its first full pass, which is the strongest thing that can be said
for the row being closed.

Fixed by `2026_11_01_120000_grant_passkey_credential_update.php` — **one column, named**, and no
`credential_id` or `user_id` UPDATE, because a changed credential id is a different key and
re-pointing a key at another account is the escalation `narrow_auth_grants` exists to refuse. Two
cases in `AuthGrantNarrowingTest`: one drives the vendor's own UPDATE statement, one pins the
grant set to **exactly** `credential, last_used_at, name, updated_at` so a later widening fails
there rather than passing quietly. Proven both ways with `REVOKE`/`GRANT` against the test
database: **2 failed** — *"Failed asserting that '42501' is null"* — and **6 passed** with it.

**4. ⛔ `navigator.serviceWorker.register()` REJECTING WAS UNCAUGHT, AND THE SCREEN LIED.**
The reconcile effect awaited `register()` and `ready` inside a bare
`void (async () => { … })()` with no `catch`, so a rejection became an unhandled promise
rejection: no state change, no honest message, and the customer left on the GRANTED alerts screen
— *"we'll buzz you"* — with no worker and therefore no push path behind it. `§4.1`'s *"honest
message"* clause forbids exactly that.

⚠ **AN ENGINE FOUND IT, AND THE ENGINE WAS RIGHT.** `one-handed.spec.ts` timed out on
`alerts.granted` on WebKit LTR and RTL, every run, while the same state passed on Chromium and
Firefox. The harness serves the page over a self-signed certificate; `ignoreHTTPSErrors` is a
Playwright option and a worker script is fetched by the browser's own NETWORK STACK, so it does
not reach that fetch — `playwright.config.ts` says so where the journey projects pass Chromium
`--ignore-certificate-errors`, a flag WebKit has no equivalent for. So the registration genuinely
failed there, reproducing what private browsing, revoked storage and a restrictive policy all
produce in production.

A device with no worker has no push path, which is what `alerts.unsupported` already means, so
the catch dispatches `permission/unsupported` and `§4.1`'s own fallback applies unchanged:
polling keeps the status screen live, the product continues, and only the buzz is lost — `O2`'s
decision honoured rather than a new one. Asserted in `orchestrator.test.tsx` with both halves:
the screen tells the truth AND the poll count still rises. Proven red by reverting the dispatch:
*"expected undefined to be 'unsupported'"*.

**5. ⚠ A VACUOUS ASSERTION, AND THE FIRST REPLACEMENT FOR IT WAS WRONG.**
`one-handed.spec.ts` ended every one of its 102 cases with

```
expect(polls).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(0)
```

which is true for every possible value, including a poller that never ran. The first replacement
asserted `polls > 0` for every state with a live session — and **54 cases went red at
`polls=0`**, because polling STARTS the moment a session resolves but has not FIRED before these
states are reached. That was an assertion about the machine's speed wearing the costume of one
about the journey. What is left is the part that is a property: `polls === 0` on the seven states
with no live session to poll, and `polls > 0` on `waiting.degraded`, which is reachable only
THROUGH a 503 poll answer. The other nine are asserted at their real cadence in `journey.test.ts`
and `pager.spec.ts`, where the clock is the subject.

**6. ⚠ `pager.spec.ts` DEMANDED THE WRONG STATE ON ONE ENGINE, EVERY RUN SINCE IT WAS WRITTEN.**
Its permission-denied case branched `if (ask.isVisible()) … else expect(unsupported)`, i.e. it
assumed an engine with no *"Allow notifications"* button must be one with no `Notification` at
all. There is a third real shape: headless Chromium reports `Notification.permission === 'denied'`
with no prompt ever shown, so the app correctly rendered `alerts.denied` — which has no ask button
either, because a retry would be a lie. The `else` branch then failed against a page behaving
exactly as specified. The expected state is now DERIVED from the engine's own answer and asserted
as one exact value, with no disjunction and nothing branching on the UI the assertion is about.
Green on all three engines afterwards.

**7. ⚠ `lighthouse-proof` NAMED THE RIGHT CHROME AND MEASURED WITH NONE — a missing `export`.**
It resolved `CHROME_PATH` from `chromium.executablePath()`, printed *Google Chrome for Testing
156.0.8078.4* at `/ms-playwright/chromium-1248/...` into its own report header, and never
exported the variable. `chrome-launcher` reads `process.env.CHROME_PATH` and Lighthouse has no
`--chrome-path` flag, so the child process searched the container, found nothing, and died on run
1 of 5 with *"The CHROME_PATH environment variable must be set"*. **A header that names the
toolchain is not the same as a measurement that used it**, which is the rank-1 brief's trap 5
turned on this task's own script.

#### ⚠ THE TWO GATES MUST NOT RUN AT THE SAME TIME, AND THAT IS `R-200`'s MECHANISM ONE LAYER OUT

`php artisan serve` (the E2E's API) uses `.env`'s `DB_DATABASE=qrpager`; the suite uses
`phpunit.xml`'s `qrpager_test`. So **Postgres is not the shared resource — Redis is**, exactly
as `R-200`'s own correction records: `TestCase::setUp`'s `clearPagerProjection()` deletes
`t:*:pager:*` and `pager:tok:*` before every test, and a pager session IS a Redis key. Running
`composer gate` while `pnpm run gate:e2e` is up would delete the E2E's live sessions
mid-journey.

They are therefore run **serially**, and that is stated here rather than discovered: a reader
who runs both at once will get a red E2E whose cause is in the other terminal.

#### `§11` ROUND ONE — 28 findings, both reviews, and what they cost

**QA: 13 findings — 1 Critical, 4 High, 4 Medium, 4 Low. SECURITY: 15 findings — 0 Critical,
0 High, 7 Medium, 8 Low.** Both reviewers resolved the diff to `a6f9a47`, base `58ca1ea`,
89 files, +19,867/−83, each in its own worktree pinned at that sha, each launched with the
read-only agent definition and the brief verbatim. **Run SEQUENTIALLY rather than in parallel**,
which is a decision and not an accident: both worktrees share this machine's one Postgres and
Redis, and `R-200`'s mechanism — `clearPagerProjection()` deleting `t:*:pager:*` before every
test — means two reviewers running `php artisan test` at once would corrupt each other's runs
and produce findings about the other's interference.

**⚠ WHAT BOTH REVIEWERS COULD NOT SEE, stated rather than left implicit:** neither subagent had
an Atlassian tool, so **QRPAGER-16's Jira comment thread was not readable by either**. Both read
the committed 979-line `docs/tickets/QRPAGER-16.md` instead, which is what `§4a` records as
relayed to the ticket as comment `10086`. A clause living only in a Jira comment and in neither
that file nor `PLAN.md`/`PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md` has not been reviewed.

**⚠ AND A REVIEWER-PROCEDURE FACT WORTH MORE THAN SOME OF THE FINDINGS:** `php artisan test`
**cannot run from a git worktree at all.** Pest derives its root from the autoloader, so with
`apps/api/vendor` symlinked every test file is treated as outside the root,
`pest()->extend(TestCase::class)->in('Feature')` never binds, and Laravel-dependent cases die
with `Container::basePath()`. A worktree whose directory name starts with a digit — which
`R-189` mandates for reviewers — fails earlier still with `Pest\Exceptions\InvalidTestClassName`.
Both reviewers hit it independently and both found a sound way round it (one ran the PHP half in
a clean checkout at the identical sha; the other extracted the guard's own detection function
and re-ran it). This is now in `§0`.

**FOUR RULINGS FROM MUHAMMAD, 2026-11-01, folded into round one rather than deferred:**

1. **SEC M-3 is a HIGH, not a Medium.** The reviewer rated it Medium on *"it needs a script on
   the origin"*; `R-171` records that `apps/web` has no response-header policy and
   `web-csp-surface.json` shows six inline scripts, which rules out a plain `script-src 'self'`
   — so the precondition is weaker than the rating assumed. Fixed so the production worker

3. **QA L-3 / `SR-5` RULED:** *"and the next notification still arrives"* must be ASSERTED.
4. **QA M-4:** the start deviation is recorded — `§0.0b`.

#### ⚠ AND THE MECHANISATION CAUGHT MY OWN FIX, WITHIN THE HOUR

`SEC L-4` offered two closures: emit the inline-script hashes the ticket claimed, or correct the
ticket. I emitted them and committed them. `tools/gate/bin/fresh-clone-proof` — a CI step as of
this round's ruling (a), which did not exist when round one started — reddened on the clone of
`80e3223`:

```
    "inlineScriptHashes": [
       "sha256-OBTN3RiyCV4Bq7dFqZ5a2pAXjnCcCYeTJMO2I/LYKeo=",
    -  "sha256-1tFSdVDj/PoKrWzqlYEq8mMK+Yr4mRirgrbBwLtpdjo=",
    -  "sha256-7Mq3N50e5xRjHPX6/UmLHAwlaBWqvLmtJzD2PraNlCo=",
    +  "sha256-Bv9hoqrrVen0YIByEWoc9BoLDlOhusY1D3FR5yMuGi0=",
    +  "sha256-xmzg8R6r8IGTTsmEo9hUGCEHPwH17cLj166q9zQzWww=",
       ...three identical...
    ]
```

**Measured, same commit, two builds: four of the six hashes are identical and EXACTLY TWO
differ** — Next's RSC payload pushes carry build-specific content. So a committed hash list is
not fragile, it is **wrong on any machine but the one that wrote it**, which is the same defect
class as QA C-1 and was caught by the step added for QA C-1.

⚠ **AND THE CORRECTED ANSWER IS WORTH MORE THAN THE HASH LIST WOULD HAVE BEEN:** a `script-src`
policy for this page **cannot be static**. It has to be emitted by the build, from that build's
own output, or by the edge as a per-response nonce. That is written into the artefact with the
numbers behind it, `R-171`'s acceptance clause is tightened to match, and the count, shape and
distinctness of the six hashes are computed and asserted on every run — so the capability is
demonstrated without pinning a build artefact. Had the hashes shipped, Task 12 would have taken
six values into a policy that breaks on its own CI.

#### `§11` ROUND TWO — 30 findings on the fix diff, and both Highs were mine

**QA: 18 findings — 0 Critical, 2 High, 9 Medium, 7 Low. SECURITY: 12 findings — 0 Critical,
1 High, 5 Medium, 6 Low.** Both resolved `git diff a6f9a47...9ed1ceb` (34 files, +4,481/−1,556),
each in its own worktree pinned at `9ed1ceb`, run sequentially for `R-200`'s reason, each left
clean. **Neither had an Atlassian tool either**, so the Jira thread is unreviewed in both rounds.

**⚠ THE TWO FINDINGS THAT MATTERED WERE BOTH INTRODUCED BY ROUND ONE'S OWN FIXES, and both
reviewers found each independently.**

**1. THE NAMED INVARIANT WAS BROKEN** (QA H-2 ≡ SEC-R2 M-1). Round one made `hasExpired()` treat
a missing expiry as expired — fail closed, correctly — and left the rotation write-back emitting
no `expiresAt`. So rotation 1 wrote a credential that `readCredential()` **purged on the next
read**: rotation 2 sent no `DELETE` for the dead endpoint and registered nothing, on the engine
with no `oldSubscription` (Firefox), which is the only reason the write-back exists. On iOS the
read never happens at all, so the raw token sat in Cache Storage with no recorded expiry —
re-opening SEC M-2's residual on the platform `R-073` calls the largest risk. `§11`'s round cap
does not cover an invariant failure, so this blocked regardless.

**2. SEC M-3's RULING WAS NOT SATISFIED** (SEC-R2 H-1 ≡ QA M-1). The ruling was *"must not be
able to read it at all — not validate it, not reach it"*, and its stated REASON was the `apiBase`
the worker sends the raw token to and writes BACK. Round one removed the cache **name** and left
the **mechanism**: `apiBase` still came from stored data, both token-bearing requests still went
to it, and it was still persisted. **And round one made it worse** — the harness page was
repointed at the production credential entry, so the planting surface got wider, not narrower
(SEC-R2 M-5). The worker now derives its API origin from its own script URL (`?api=`, set by the
page from its build-time constant), and writes no `apiBase` back at all.

**⚠ AND FIVE ROUND-ONE FIXES HAD NO TEST AT ALL** — both reviewers listed them separately (QA
M-3, L-1; SEC-R2 M-3, L-1, L-2). The navigate whitelist, the `fresh.ok` guard, `notificationclick`,
the raw-payload suppression and the POST-failure branch were all correct by reading and asserted
by nothing. The shim gained a fetch-outcome knob, a `fetch`/`activate` event path and a report of
the stores it leaves behind, because the write-back and the failure branch were **unreachable by
any case**.

**⚠ THE MECHANISM I ADDED TO STOP H-4 WAS ITSELF DEAD CODE** (QA M-4 ≡ SEC-R2 M-4).
`check-records`' currency check computed two values and discarded them (`void head`) behind a
success line claiming it ran. Both reviewers proved it the same way: falsify a committed total,
watch the script report *"every committed transcript is current and green"*. **And my first
replacement was wrong the same way** — keyed on "changed in HEAD", so one further commit made it
inert again. It now checks every matched transcript, exempts `-baseline-` names, holds only the
ticket `§0` names to the current suite, and compares the PHP count alone — `vitest list` reports
616 against a run of 812 because it does not expand parameterised cases, so comparing it would
fire on every honest transcript.

**⚠ AND THE NEW SHELL RULE FOUND FIVE MORE OF QA H-1's FAMILY ON ITS FIRST RUN**, in
`three-green-runs` (twice), `fresh-clone-proof` and `lighthouse-proof` (twice) — including the
two lines that extract the test counts and the failure list, so a green run with no failure lines
would have aborted the loop that exists to report it.

**⛔ AND QA H-1 FORCED A CORRECTION TO THIS RECORD.** `free_port`'s pipeline assignment under
`pipefail` aborted the EXIT trap, so `gate:e2e` exited 1 after printing `e2e: green` and three
ports were never freed. `gate:e2e` **also** exits non-zero when the Lighthouse median is under the
bar, so the builder saw `EXIT=1` on a 314-passed/0-failed run and attributed it to `R-205`. Both
produce the same code and nothing distinguished them. **The suite tally was real; the gate's exit
status was never once observed to be 0 before this round.** Measured after the fix: `EXIT=0`, all
four ports freed, and `EXIT=1` with the `|| true` removed.

#### ⚠ THE SECOND PUSH WAS FIRED WITH `renotify`, NOT `markReady`, AND THAT CORRECTION CONFIRMED THREE `§4` CLAUSES IN ONE RUN

The instruction was *"re-run `markReady` on a fresh session"*. That would not have worked, and the way
it would have failed is the instructive part:

1. **`push_subscriptions.pager_session_id` binds a subscription to ONE session.** A fresh session
   carries no subscription, so the dispatcher would have reported **`delivered: 0`** — and on a locked
   phone that reads as *iOS did not deliver it*, which is a false negative pointing at the platform
   when the fault is the harness. The run would have been recorded as a failure of the thing it exists
   to prove.
2. **`markReady` on the SAME session would correctly have sent NOTHING.** `§4 › Realtime`: *"`markReady`
   is idempotent. A retry never double-notifies."* The session was already `ready`, so the idempotency
   clause — which exists to stop a double-notify — would have blocked the deliberate second one.
3. **`renotify` is the staff action for exactly this**, and `§3` row 10 names it. It enqueued a second
   outbox row against the same session and the same subscription.

So one run confirmed the **session-bound subscription**, **`markReady`'s idempotency** and
**`renotify`'s distinctness** — three clauses, from a correction to the method rather than from a test.

#### ⛔ THE FINDING WORTH MORE THAN THE PUSH: THE INSTALL PATH TOOK THREE ATTEMPTS, AND ALL THREE FAILURES WERE iOS BEHAVIOURS NOBODY HAD WRITTEN DOWN

Muhammad's ruling: *"that is the finding `QRPAGER-24` existed to produce, and it is worth more than the
push itself: Task 9's install guidance has to survive all three."* `§4.1` asks the *Enable alerts*
screen for **"iOS Home-Screen install path as a first-class flow"**, and a flow written without these
three facts would have shipped broken to every iPhone customer.

| attempt | what was tried | why it failed on the device |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | The documented `#t=<token>` fragment, with the token persisted to `localStorage` on first read in Safari | **(i) An installed web app launches at the MANIFEST'S `start_url`, never at the bookmarked URL** — `start_url` was `/harness/push`, so the fragment could not survive the install. **(ii) A Home-Screen app's storage is PARTITIONED from Safari's**, so the `localStorage` write made in Safari was invisible to the installed app. The page's own comment had reasoned (i) correctly and then assumed (ii) away |
| **2** | A per-session manifest (`/harness/manifest?t=…`) whose `start_url` carries the token, with the page repointing `<link rel="manifest">` client-side | **iOS did not honour the repointed link.** Two sufficient reasons: Safari reads that link from the **HTML as served**, so a post-load JS rewrite is unreliable; and **Safari caches a manifest per ORIGIN**, so attempt 1's token-less manifest was very likely still in use. Verified working in headless Chromium, which is exactly why it is recorded — a green browser probe proved nothing about iOS |
| **3** | ✅ **A text field in the installed app.** Paste the token, validate with the GENERATED `isWellFormedPagerToken`, store in that context's own storage | **Worked first time.** Deterministic, with no iOS behaviour to guess at |

**THE RULING BEHIND ATTEMPT 3, and it is the generalisable half:** *the install path's token transport is
NOT the thing under test.* The harness exists to prove one fact — a push from the real dispatcher reaches
an installed iPhone — and the token merely has to BE in the standalone context. Two attempts were spent
guessing at Safari's manifest behaviour, which is the incidental mechanism `PROJECT_INSTRUCTIONS.md §8`
says to replace with the strongest one available. **`R-214`** carries the consequence for Task 9's
install guidance.

⚠ **AND THE HAND-WRITTEN TOKEN REGEX WAS A SECOND, LOOSER SOURCE.** Attempts 2 and 3 each validated the
token with `/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{8,64}$/` written inline — twice — while `PAGER_TOKEN_LENGTH` is **22**. A
truncated paste would have been accepted at the field and then failed at the API with a 404 naming
nothing. Replaced with the generated `isWellFormedPagerToken`; a 10-character paste is now refused at
the field, measured.

**THE SECOND HALF OF THE INVARIANT — no call site's radius ROLE changed in the move — and this table is how it is falsifiable.** The slot a site used under Direction B is not evidence of its role; what it *is* decides. Five sites sat in the control slot and are not interactive, and one sat in the surfaces slot and is a button.

| call site | Direction B slot | Rail role | why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `.qr-button` | `--radius-8` | **control** | a button |
| `.qr-field__input` | `--radius-8` | **control** | an input |
| `.qr-staff-filter__toggle` | `--radius-8` | **control** | `inline-flex` toggle, interactive |
| `.qr-ready__acknowledge` | `--radius-16` | **control** | **a button in the surfaces slot — the site that proves slot ≠ role** |
| `.qr-card` | `--radius-16` | surface | a card |
| `.qr-kds__order` | `--radius-16` | surface | an order card |
| `.pg-install` | `--radius-16` | surface | an install sheet, bordered, `space-16` padding |
| `.qr-staff-state` | `--radius-16` | surface | a state panel, `space-32`/`space-24` padding |
| `.qr-staff-list__item` | `--radius-8` | surface | a list row container, `space-16` padding — **not interactive** |
| `.qr-staff-secret` | `--radius-8` | surface | a block that displays a secret, `space-16` padding |
| `.qr-staff-warning` | `--radius-8` | surface | a notice box, `space-16` padding |
| `.pg-banner` | `--radius-8` | surface | a bordered banner |
| `.qr-badge` | `--radius-8` | surface | an `inline-block` chip, `space-4`/`space-8`, 13px — a printed label, not a control |
| `.qr-staff__role` | `--radius-8` | surface | the same chip shape |
| `.qr-progress` | `--radius-8` | surface | a progress track — nothing to touch |

**The rule that decided the three genuinely ambiguous ones** (`.qr-badge`, `.qr-staff__role`, `.qr-progress`): **radius signals interactivity.** 4px is the affordance; a label or a track is not a control, so it takes the printed 2px. Flipping any one of them is a single word in one stylesheet.

**Filament's own names map by role too:** `sm` and `md` → control (its buttons and inputs), `lg` → surface (its panels). **`xl` has no consumer in this repository** — no `rounded-xl` in any blade, component or stylesheet — and is **kept, mapped to surface**, because Filament's own CSS may `@apply` it in a release nobody here has read and an undefined property would fall back to a cleared namespace: no radius at all. The `rounded-lg` (9×) and `rounded-md` (1×) uses in `studio/builder.blade.php`, `studio/domains.blade.php` and `studio/media.blade.php` follow from that map and needed no edit.

⚠ **AND THE SUITE GAINED THE ASSERTION THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT THE MOTION DEFECT.** `a11y.spec.ts` checked the spinner's animation NAME and never its duration, so `--motion-entrance` taking Rail's `120ms` — eight turns a second — would have passed every check in the repository. It now asserts the resolved `0.8s`, beside the existing proof that `prefers-reduced-motion` resolves both durations to exactly `0ms` and removes the animation outright.

| `pnpm gate` | **1204 Vitest, 103 browser cases**; its one red is `records:check`, which reads this commit's own `§0` | `63f206f` | `storage/logs/gate-frontend-20261108T170703Z.log` |
| `fresh-clone-proof` | **GREEN — all 13 steps in a clone sharing nothing with the working tree** | `94a52a2` | `docs/tickets/QRPAGER-37-fresh-clone.txt`, `EXIT=0`. Run BEFORE the push, per `R-252` |

**THE INVARIANT IS A TEST.** `StudioMediaDropZoneTest` asserts the grid carries **every column the table carried** — name, type, size, dimensions, delete — by value, plus the thumbnail the table could not show. A redesign that quietly drops the file size is a redesign that lost something, and nothing else in the suite would have said so. 3 cases, 15 assertions; the 20 existing media tests still pass.

⚠⚠ **WHY THE FILE INPUT IS HAND-ROLLED, AND WHY A FUTURE SESSION MUST NOT "FIX" IT.** Recorded here at the owner's instruction, because a commit message is not where this belongs: **Filament's `FileUpload` component writes the file to a disk itself**, which would put bytes in the object store **without them ever passing `InspectedImage`** — Task 7's control that checks an image *by its contents, not by its name*. A later session reading *"we hand-rolled the file input"* without this sentence would helpfully replace it with the framework component and silently remove a security control. So the page keeps a plain `<input type="file">`, and `StudioMediaDropZoneTest` asserts it is still there.

**The drop zone is a `<label for>`**, not a div with a click handler: a label already opens the picker on click and from the keyboard, so the zone needs no key handler of its own and cannot become a mouse-only target. The input is `sr-only peer`, never `hidden` — `hidden` removes it from the tab order — and `peer-focus-visible:` puts the ring on the zone, where the eye is. **Measured in the browser: the ring resolves VISIBLE while the input holds focus.**

**The thumbnail is the panel's own `filament.studio.preview.asset` route**, which already serves a tenant's bytes under the panel's authorisation: no new surface, no public URL, nothing reaching the object store directly. `alt=""` is deliberate — the filename is visible text beside it, so a non-empty alt would be announced twice.

⚠ **THREE GATES CAUGHT WHAT THE BROWSER COULD NOT**, and each is a control working: `lint:panel` refused `min-h-[44px]` and `h-[160px]` as `D3` arbitrary values — both also **redundant**, since `targets.css` already sizes `.fi-btn` from `--target-min`; `panel.spec` requires every spacing class a blade uses to be pinned to a **measured** px, so `gap-8`, `gap-16`, `p-12` and `p-32` were added there; and the per-tile Delete needed a `targets.css` selector because it is a **button in a grid cell**, not inline text in a sentence, so that file's WCAG 2.5.8 exception does not cover it.

**A platform admin is now seeded** — `admin@qrpager.test` / `platform-admin-not-a-secret`, a **fixed** address unlike every other account in that fixture, because it is written down for a human to type and must survive a re-run. **It holds no membership**, since `§4 › Tenancy` says a platform admin sees that a restaurant exists and cannot see inside it. Its first version used `updateOrInsert` and Postgres refused the re-run with `23503`: that helper passes the same values to the update, so it tried to rewrite the row's `id` while `tenant_provisionings` still referenced it. **An id is the one column an idempotent upsert must never touch.**
